Bitget intends to acquire the company through its interest in Thailand’s BTGT Management.
GMO Internet and its subsidiary GMO-Z.com Holdings will sell their entire stake in the exchange to BTGT Management or its designated buyer alongside other shareholders.
The transaction remains subject to regulatory approval and other closing conditions.
Gracy Chen, CEO of Bitget, said,

Our priority is to develop the right operational foundation while bringing Bitget’s global experience and capabilities to the market.”
Once the deal is completed and regulators approve the change of control, Bitget plans to introduce its trading platform to Thai users in compliance with local regulations.

articles.title: 5 priority actions to enhance the position of Vietnamese wood and increase export value. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: 5 priority actions to enhance the position of Vietnamese wood and increase export value.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Large potential but increasing competitive pressure.
 In 2025, exports of wood and wood products are expected to reach approximately $17.2 billion. In the first nine months of 2026, this figure is projected to reach approximately $13.43 billion, a 6.3% increase compared to the same period of the previous year.
 At the trade promotion briefing conference in October 2026, held on the afternoon of October 20th with the theme "Diversifying markets, promoting the export of Vietnamese wood and furniture products," Mr. Phung Quoc Man, Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City Handicraft and Wood Processing Association (HAWA), stated that Vietnamese wood products are present in 167 countries and territories. Vietnam currently ranks second in the world for furniture exports, after China , with a diverse supply capacity ranging from home, office, and outdoor furniture to products for construction projects and hotels.
 According to Mr. Ngo Sy Hoai, Vice President and General Secretary of the Vietnam Wood and Forest Products Association, the wood industry has formed a relatively complete ecosystem from forest planting, harvesting, processing to export. There are approximately 6,000 businesses operating in the industry nationwide, of which more than 3,500 focus on exports, including over 700 foreign-invested enterprises (FDI).
 However, the industry remains heavily reliant on the US market, which typically accounts for over 50% of export revenue. Tariff policies and trade protection measures in this market are putting pressure on businesses. High logistics costs, traceability requirements, and regulations on preventing forest degradation also pose increasing challenges. 
 Mr. Le Hoang Tai, Deputy Director of the Trade Promotion Department (Ministry of Industry and Trade), believes that diversifying markets is not only about seeking more orders but also about enhancing product value and competitiveness. Businesses need to consolidate traditional markets, exploit potential markets, and at the same time understand customer needs, import conditions, and appropriate access channels.
 Several markets are opening up notable opportunities. In the Netherlands , in the first nine months of 2026, Vietnam's exports of wood and wood products reached US$138 million, an 86% increase compared to the same period the previous year. The Netherlands is also a logistics and distribution hub for goods entering the EU. Meanwhile, the Indian furniture market is estimated to be worth approximately US$22 billion, projected to reach US$30-40 billion in the near future, with an average annual growth rate of 8-10%.
 However, according to Mr. Bui Trung Thuong, Vietnam's Commercial Counselor in India , India is also a difficult market to access due to protectionist policies for domestic production and technical barriers. The most-favored-nation import duty on furniture is 20%, while goods from countries with free trade agreements with India, including ASEAN, enjoy a duty rate of 0-5%. Businesses also need to be aware of trade defense measures and certification requirements from the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS). 
 Mr. Bui Trung Thuong - Commercial Counselor of Vietnam in India. (Screenshot)
 Five priorities to elevate the status of Vietnamese wood.
 To enhance his position in the global value chain, Mr. Ngo Sy Hoai proposed five priority actions.
 Firstly, diversify markets, customers, and sales channels, reducing dependence on a single market. In the US, businesses need to maintain market share, manage tariff and origin risks, and seek new markets, including niche markets. In the EU and UK, they should leverage free trade agreements; in Japan and South Korea , they should expand opportunities for interior and exterior products. Businesses should also explore potential in the Middle East, ASEAN, Australia, and other markets.
 Secondly, investing in design, technology, artificial intelligence (AI), productivity, and human resource skills will gradually shift from contract manufacturing to proactively developing products and owning the brand.
 Thirdly, developing large-timber plantations ensures the legality and traceability of raw materials, meeting the increasingly high demands of importing markets.
 Fourth, build the brand of Vietnamese wood and furniture, and develop direct distribution channels to enhance the value that businesses receive from exported products.
 Fifth, harmoniously link product groups from wood chips, pellets, wood panels to furniture, thereby increasing the value obtained per cubic meter of wood.
 According to Mr. Hoai, the industry needs to shift from purely OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer) to ODM (Original Design Manufacturer), aiming for brand ownership. The goal is to create "Made in Vietnam" products, designed by Vietnamese people, bearing Vietnamese brands, and trusted by international customers. 
 Mr. Phung Quoc Man - Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City Handicraft and Wood Processing Association (HAWA). (Screenshot)  To achieve these priorities, the supportive role of the Vietnamese trade office system abroad is crucial. Mr. Phung Quoc Man suggested that trade offices provide focused information on market needs, customer segments, distribution channels, and import requirements; verify partners; connect businesses with importers and retailers; and monitor the cooperation process from sample submission and quotation to negotiation and order signing.
 Associations and businesses also need to coordinate closely with the Trade Promotion and Business Office to promote production capabilities, attract international buyers to Vietnam to attend specialized trade fairs and exhibitions, and conduct factory surveys.
 According to Mr. Le Hoang Tai, market diversification needs to go hand in hand with enhancing competitiveness and participating more deeply in the value-creating stages of the supply chain. This is also a direction consistent with the "Go Global" program for the period 2026–2030, approved by Decision No. 626/QD-TTg dated June 4, 2026.
 The ultimate goal is not only to bring more wood products to the international market, but also to help Vietnamese brands become more clearly recognized, enabling businesses to be more proactive in the value chain and benefit proportionally to their production capacity.
 Nguyet Minh

articles.title: Vietnam-Singapore trade surges 46.8% in first nine months - Báo Cần Thơ
articles.summary: Vietnam-Singapore trade surges 46.8% in first nine months  Báo Cần Thơ
articles.full_text:
Illustrative photo (Photo: VNA)
  
 Trade between Vietnam and Singapore grew strongly in the first nine months of 2026, with two-way turnover reaching nearly 42.8 billion SGD (33.4 billion USD), up 46.8% year on year.
The growth exceeded Singapore’s overall foreign trade increase of 36.9%. Vietnam remained Singapore’s 10th-largest trading partner, with its share of Singapore’s total trade rising from 2.9% to 3.1%.
Singapore’s imports from Vietnam surged 123.2% to 19.4 billion SGD, more than three times the 35.7% growth in its overall imports. Vietnam’s share of Singapore’s total imports consequently rose from 1.8% to 3%.
Meanwhile, Singapore’s exports to Vietnam increased 14.3% to 23.4 billion SGD. Of this, domestically produced goods accounted for 6.4 billion SGD, up 15.1%, while re-exports reached nearly 17 billion SGD, up 14%.
The strong momentum continued in September, when bilateral trade rose 61.6% year on year to nearly 5.2 billion SGD. Singapore’s exports to Vietnam reached nearly 3 billion SGD, up 35.6%, while imports from Vietnam exceeded 2.2 billion SGD, an increase of 115.9%.
Including re-exports, Singapore recorded a trade surplus of 4 billion SGD with Vietnam during the nine-month period, according to Singapore’s figures. However, when only domestically produced Singaporean goods are counted, Singapore recorded a trade deficit of 12.9 billion SGD.
The figures indicate that Vietnam is becoming an increasingly important source of goods for Singapore’s distribution and re-export networks, rather than simply a market for goods shipped through the city-state.
Data from Enterprise Singapore showed that electrical machinery, equipment and parts (HS 85), together with mineral fuels, oils and related products (HS 27), remained Singapore’s two largest export categories to Vietnam. Combined exports in these categories exceeded 15.1 billion SGD, accounting for 64.6% of Singapore’s total exports to Vietnam.
On the import side, HS 85 products also remained Singapore’s largest import category from Vietnam, reaching 9.5 billion SGD, up 118.8% and accounting for 49.2% of total imports from Vietnam.
The Vietnam Trade Office in Singapore attributed the growth partly to the Singapore’s investment cycle in artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductors, which is boosting electronics production, exports and re-exports while increasing demand for machinery, equipment and components from regional manufacturing centres, including Vietnam.
Rising Singaporean imports of HS 84 and HS 85 products from Vietnam highlight the country’s growing role in regional electronics and technology supply chains, complementing Vietnam’s manufacturing and assembly capacity with Singapore’s strengths in distribution, re-exports, finance and logistics.

articles.title: Supporting industries: We cannot remain outside the FDI supply chain forever. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Supporting industries: We cannot remain outside the FDI supply chain forever.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| Vietnamese businesses are still limited by technological capabilities, production scale, and management expertise. | 
 According to Mr. Chu Viet Cuong, Acting Director of the Center for Industrial Development Support - Ministry of Industry and Trade , the FDI sector contributes up to 77% of export turnover and accounts for 82.8% of investment capital in the processing and manufacturing industry. Meanwhile, foreign added value in Vietnam's exports reaches 48.5%. The proportion of Vietnamese enterprises participating in global value chains is also trending downwards.
 These figures show that despite becoming an important link in the international production network, Vietnam has not yet mastered many high-value-added stages. Large export volumes do not necessarily translate into commensurate domestic value, as a significant portion of raw materials, components, and technology still depend on external sources.
 This situation is clearly reflected in the localization rates in some key industries. The electronics industry has reached approximately 35%, mechanical engineering 25-30%, while the passenger car industry only reaches 15-20%. This means there is still enormous potential for the development of supporting industries, but the ability of domestic businesses to take advantage of these opportunities remains limited by technological capabilities, production scale, and management skills.
 Notably, a survey of 7,000 businesses revealed that over 30% still use manual machinery, over 50% use semi-automatic equipment, while the rate of robot adoption is less than 10%. Regarding quality and environmental standards, only 20% of businesses have ISO 9000 certification and 9% have ISO 14000 certification.
 This isn't simply a matter of lacking modern machinery. In the global supply chain, suppliers must simultaneously meet multiple requirements regarding quality, cost, delivery schedule, traceability, and product consistency. A single flawed link can jeopardize a partner's entire production plan.
 Therefore, Vietnamese businesses wanting to participate more deeply in the supply chain cannot simply rely on networking opportunities. Supply capacity must be demonstrated through actual quality, on-time delivery, and cost competitiveness. Without addressing these fundamental limitations, opportunities for cooperation with FDI businesses are likely to remain limited to networking meetings and conferences, failing to translate into long-term orders.
 Experts believe that developing a supplier network in Vietnam benefits both FDI and domestic businesses. For multinational corporations, local sourcing optimizes logistics costs, shortens delivery times, reduces reliance on lengthy supply routes, and enhances responsiveness to market fluctuations. Meanwhile, Vietnamese supporting industries gain access to technology, improve management processes, increase labor productivity, and develop human resources to meet international demands. More importantly, becoming a supplier for large corporations can lay the groundwork for businesses to expand their customer base, upgrade products, and gradually participate in higher value-added stages of production.
 However, this benefit does not appear automatically. The gap in technological level and production standards makes it difficult for many domestic businesses to meet the requirements of FDI corporations. Meanwhile, if supplier selection is based solely on immediate cost, without support programs for capacity building, the process of forming a domestic supply network will struggle to achieve the expected results.
 Therefore, the link between the two regions needs to go beyond mere buying and selling activities to aim for long-term cooperation. FDI enterprises need to enhance information sharing on technical standards, quality requirements, and order plans, creating conditions for domestic suppliers to proactively invest. Assessment, training, and process improvement consulting programs should also be emphasized to help Vietnamese businesses gradually meet the requirements of their partners. 
|  | 
| Strengthening linkages between FDI enterprises and domestic enterprises is considered a crucial solution to improve the localization rate. | 
 Conversely, domestic businesses must proactively change their production mindset, considering consistent quality and delivery capacity as vital conditions for survival. Investing in technology, standardizing processes, training technical workers, and improving design capabilities cannot be done only when orders are placed, but must become a long-term development strategy.
 To promote supporting industries, the Ministry of Industry and Trade has identified the need for a comprehensive implementation of solutions including market development, financial support, technological innovation, improved design capabilities, and selective investment attraction. In particular, strengthening linkages between FDI enterprises and domestic businesses is considered a crucial solution to improve the localization rate and gradually form a sustainable supply chain network.
 However, networking programs are only effective when accompanied by sufficiently specific support mechanisms. Businesses wishing to become suppliers often have to invest in machinery, upgrade production lines, build quality control systems, and meet necessary certifications. This is a significant investment, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises with limited financial resources.
 Mr. Tran Van Tan, Deputy Director of the Department of Credit for Economic Sectors - State Bank of Vietnam, shared that thanks to the attention and coordination of local Party committees and authorities at all levels, from 2014 to the present, the banking sector nationwide has organized over 1,500 meetings and dialogues with businesses, thereby resolving difficulties for nearly 195,000 businesses. The total amount of new loans committed by banks reached nearly 2,500,000 billion VND, with common interest rates at 6-9% per year for short-term loans and 9-11% per year for medium and long-term loans. Managers and businesses alike affirm that this connection program helps businesses and banks understand each other better, share difficulties, and develop together.
 Bank-business linkage programs have yielded positive results in supporting access to credit. However, for capital flows to truly boost supporting industries, credit solutions that are more tailored to the specific production characteristics and order cycles of businesses are needed. Credit assessment based on business plans, cash flow, supply contracts, and order fulfillment capabilities could open up more opportunities for businesses with production capacity but limited collateral. Simultaneously, programs that finance technological innovation, equipment upgrades, and compliance with international standards should be encouraged.
 Besides capital, support policies should also aim at establishing a database of domestic suppliers, making it easier for FDI corporations to search, evaluate, and select partners. Supply-demand matching activities need to shift from introducing businesses to clearly identifying component needs, technical standards, supply capabilities, and the fulfillment timeline of each supplier.

articles.title: Article 2: House prices have fallen, but the real estate market remains "frozen". - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Article 2: House prices have fallen, but the real estate market remains "frozen".  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
The latest research data from Dat Xanh Services' Institute for Economic , Financial, and Real Estate Research (FERI) shows that real estate prices in the third quarter of 2026 recorded a widespread downward trend ranging from 5% to 20% compared to the second quarter of 2026. This price reduction was evident across all segments and geographical regions.
 For high-rise apartments, selling prices decreased nationwide. In the southern region, apartment prices recorded a downward adjustment of 5-10%, bringing the average price range to between 36-145 million VND/m².
 Prices for low-rise housing in urban development projects in the South have decreased by 10-15%, currently ranging from 50-320 million VND/m². Even the land market – a preferred segment for investors – has also fallen by 10-15%, bringing prices down to around 25-135 million VND/m².
 Despite price levels stabilizing and declining significantly, market liquidity remains very low, with no signs of a strong return of capital. The situation of "prices falling but trading remaining frozen" reflects a paradox stemming from deep-seated bottlenecks in capital costs and market sentiment.
 The core reason for the continued liquidity bottleneck is the high cost of capital. Ms. Vo Nhat Lieu, General Director of BrandLift ASIA Project Development Consulting Company, pointed out that current mortgage interest rates are approximately three times higher than they were two years ago (when preferential interest rates were only around 6% per year). The soaring financial costs have led to a significant decline in the percentage of customers using bank leverage to purchase real estate.
 Meanwhile, homebuyers are particularly apprehensive about the risks of floating interest rates after the promotional period. Even if the listed price of the project is reduced or the developer offers many gifts, the pressure of monthly principal and interest payments still exceeds the financial capacity of the majority of middle-income families.
 From a banking and finance perspective, real estate finance expert Nguyen Viet Hung believes that the room for a rapid and widespread reduction in real estate lending interest rates in the short term is limited. This is because lending interest rates depend not only on the desire to support the real estate market but also on the cost of capital mobilization, system liquidity, inflation, exchange rates, and the safety objectives of each bank. Therefore, even if the legal issues of many projects are resolved, it is difficult to expect a rapid and widespread reduction in floating interest rates.
 However, the removal of legal obstacles will significantly change how banks perceive the risks of a project.
 A project with clear legal status, eligible for implementation and business operations, a financially capable investor, good actual construction progress, and a clear cash flow will have a lower level of risk than a project with legal issues. This makes the project easier to assess for credit and more likely to access favorable loan conditions.
 Instead of understanding that there will be a "separate credit limit" for all projects that have just had their legal procedures cleared, it should be understood that real estate credit will increasingly be differentiated according to project quality and borrower quality.
 The bank will focus on key questions such as: What is the legal status of this project? Will it generate cash flow? Is there real demand for the product? Does the developer have the financial capacity to implement the project?
 "I believe this is a positive change. Capital flows don't necessarily need to pour into the entire market, but should flow into projects with complete legal frameworks, products that meet real needs, and have good absorption capacity," said Mr. Nguyen Viet Hung. 
 Besides financial barriers, the defensive mindset of homebuyers is also a factor causing the market to stagnate. Witnessing continuous downward adjustments in property prices, a "wait for further price drops" mentality has spread. Buyers are actually making decisions very slowly because they fear buying at a short-term peak or facing risks if the developer fails to complete the project due to cash flow depletion.
 For investors, the high cost of capital has stifled the returns from short-term trading. In the context of abundant supply and a illiquid secondary market, individual investors are no longer keen on using high leverage.
 However, experts assert that this period is not entirely "frozen" for all segments. The market is witnessing strong differentiation: projects with complete legal documentation, guaranteed construction progress, and affordable prices are still attracting interest from cash-strapped customers.
 The liquidity bottleneck will only truly be resolved when lending interest rates fall to a reasonable level and real estate prices adjust to a point of equilibrium with people's actual income.
 According to Ms. Vo Nhat Lieu, the end of 2026-2027 may not necessarily be a "supply glut" in the sense of excess housing. The deciding factor is liquidity. When purchasing power cannot keep up, developers will postpone sales launches, divide the inventory into smaller units, or increase incentives. Therefore, the large supply planned may not appear on the market all at once.
 A more worrying risk is that the products produced don't match buyers' budgets. The supply may seem abundant, but if the majority are high-end or overpriced, the majority still won't find suitable homes. In short, the market may have an oversupply of products but a shortage of purchasing power, and affordable housing will still be lacking.
 Therefore, 2026–2027 is likely to be a period of strong cash flow and developer capacity consolidation, rather than a pure oversupply crisis. Businesses with clear legal standing, realistic timelines, reasonable prices, and sound finances will maintain liquidity. Conversely, businesses that overvalue, rely on customer deposits, or lack sufficient resources for implementation will face significant pressure.
 In the long term, legal reforms must go hand in hand with restructuring the supply chain and making long-term credit more accessible. If the projects that are streamlined remain primarily high-end, while social housing and affordable commercial housing do not increase accordingly, then supply and demand will continue to be mismatched. The core question is not how much supply the market has, but whether that supply meets demand, at the right price, and at the right time.
 Meanwhile, high interest rates and tight credit limits are making both investors and homebuyers more cautious. Recent transactions show a clear decrease in the percentage of buyers borrowing to purchase properties compared to before.
 Investors are using less leverage and prioritizing products with interest rate subsidies or flexible payment schedules. Buyers looking for a place to live are being more cautious due to concerns about debt repayment pressure, especially since current interest rates are about three times higher than they were more than two years ago, when they were only around 6%. Therefore, demand remains, but buyers are making decisions more slowly and are more sensitive to selling prices, interest rates, and payment policies.
 According to Ms. Vo Nhat Lieu, it is necessary to design long-term credit packages with stable interest rates for first-time homebuyers, social housing, and affordable commercial housing; especially, additional packages for first-time homebuyers are needed. This can be implemented immediately to stimulate demand. For example, in 2025, BIDV launched a 40,000 billion VND support package for homebuyers under 35 years old with an interest rate of only 5.5%.
 At the same time, priority should be given to credit limits for projects with complete legal documentation, rapid and on-schedule implementation, and affordable pricing. Regulation should also clearly distinguish between credit serving real housing needs and speculative capital, controlling high leverage instead of tightening across the board, thereby directing capital to the segments where the market is lacking.
 Besides price reductions, developers need to share the financial burden with buyers, as many buyers are unable to purchase not because of high prices but because of a lack of cash at the time of payment. Practical solutions include reducing the down payment to around 5-15%, spreading payments according to the actual construction progress, and providing interest rate support for the first 24-48 months.
 In addition, businesses can expand their customer base through a lease-to-own model, renting out the property first and then deducting the rent from the purchase price. They can also establish a brokerage channel to facilitate reselling the property on the secondary market, making it easier for existing buyers to resell, thus reducing the problem of low-priced inventory dumps. Finally, developers should collaborate with banks to design a customized loan package for the project, shortening disbursement times and reducing or waiving early repayment penalties, giving borrowers peace of mind and encouraging them to settle their loans early when they have the funds.

articles.title: PM orders cut in intermediary costs to ease housing, fuel, and healthcare price pressures - Vietnam Economic Times
articles.summary: PM orders cut in intermediary costs to ease housing, fuel, and healthcare price pressures  Vietnam Economic Times
articles.full_text:
During a National Assembly group discussion session on socio-economic development and the state budget on October 18, Prime Minister Le Minh Hung underscored the urgent need to enhance productivity, reinforce competitiveness, and lower production costs to address upward cost pressures.
To this end, the government is conducting comprehensive reviews across real estate, land management, petroleum, electricity, pharmaceuticals, medical devices, and agriculture to eliminate unwarranted markups, cut intermediary layers, and raise regulatory oversight efficiency.
Regarding petroleum products, the Prime Minister noted that amid a 65% to 90% surge in global prices, domestic prices could have spiked by as much as 80% absent targeted tax interventions, which would have triggered secondary round price shocks across a wide range of goods. Proactive tax relief measures have successfully maintained domestic fuel prices below regional peers, dampening broader cost pressures.
The government has also ordered strict penalties for misconduct in the pharmaceutical and medical equipment sectors, rooting out unnecessary middlemen markups that inflate costs for patients.
In the power sector, structural reviews of state utility enterprises are underway to optimize operations and reduce generating and distribution costs.
The PM emphasized the necessity of guaranteeing stable power supplies, preserving electricity tariff stability, and curbing price volatility across essential commodities. High economic growth must be anchored by macroeconomic stability, he warned, cautioning that unchecked inflation would erode economic gains and diminish the real benefits delivered to citizens.
On budgetary management, the government in 2026 waived approximately VND235 trillion ($9 billion) in revenues and deferred an additional VND125 trillion ($4.8 billion) to preserve liquidity for businesses and household enterprises. Despite these tax relief packages, total full-year state budget revenue is projected to exceed VND3 quadrillion (over $116 billion), up 14% year-on-year, with domestic revenues contributing an estimated VND2.6 quadrillion (over $100 billion).
According to the Government leader, robust revenue collection reflects the fundamental resilience of the economy while simultaneously supporting businesses and driving growth. Nevertheless, for investment capital to translate into tangible economic outcomes, key national priority infrastructure projects must operate efficiently, ensuring that citizens and enterprises fully benefit from upgraded connectivity.

A 12-year monument to mistrust, the China-North Korea bridge is open – locking in Beijing’s edge over Moscow and Washington, says this academic.
BOSTON, Massachusetts: For 12 years, the New Yalu River Bridge stood as the most expensive dead end in Northeast Asia. Completed by China in 2014 at a cost of US$350 million, the sleek four-lane cable-stayed span stretched across the border from Dandong only to terminate abruptly in unpaved North Korean farmland outside Sinuiju.
Now, after more than a decade of false starts, Beijing and Pyongyang officially opened the crossing to traffic on Oct 15.
Why open a 12-year-old bridge now? The answer goes well beyond border logistics. By turning on the tap of high-capacity commercial traffic, Beijing is physically retiring the era of sanctions-led pressure on North Korea – and ensuring that neither Moscow’s wartime courtship nor Washington’s appetite for fresh summiteering dilutes China’s position as the indispensable arbiter on the Korean Peninsula.
For a decade, the dormant bridge served as a barometer of quiet friction between the two socialist neighbours. After China finished the main span in 2014, disputes over who would pay for the North Korean customs complex and entry roads stalled the project.
Then came Pyongyang’s escalating nuclear tests, Beijing’s decision to back harsh United Nations Security Council sanctions in 2017, and finally Kim Jong-un’s draconian pandemic-era border closure. Opening a four-lane trade artery while the UN sanctions regime was at its peak would have been diplomatically awkward for Beijing and quarantined by Pyongyang.
That calculus has now inverted. Beijing has already dropped the word “denuclearisation” from its public diplomacy with Pyongyang, shifting from viewing North Korea’s nuclear arsenal as a proliferation liability to treating it as a durable buffer that ties down American military attention.
Once Beijing accepted a nuclear-armed North Korea as a baseline reality, keeping its primary commercial artery padlocked no longer made strategic sense.
The opening is the culmination of a methodical normalisation: cross-border truck freight resumed in 2023, the Beijing-Pyongyang passenger train restarted in March 2026 after a six-year suspension, and now the ageing single-lane Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge – built by Imperial Japan in 1937 – is being supplemented by a modern highway designed for heavy containerised freight.
THE RUSSIA CARD
Yet timing in Northeast Asia is never accidental, and two popular misreadings of this moment deserve to be challenged.
The first is the widespread notion that Kim Jong-un successfully used his high-profile military partnership with Vladimir Putin to strong-arm a reluctant China into re-engaging.
On the surface, the optics are seductive. Just five weeks ago, on Sep 7, North Korea and Russia inaugurated their first road bridge across the Tumen River, a project that raced from groundbreaking in April 2025 to ribbon-cutting in roughly 16 months.
Compared with China’s 12-year delay on the Yalu, Moscow’s sprint looked like a triumph of wartime expediency.
But optics should not be confused with economic gravity. China still accounts for over 98 per cent of North Korea’s official external trade. That single figure remains the defining reality of Pyongyang’s external relations – regardless of how “deep and close” its booming alignment with Moscow may appear to outside observers.
Moscow can supply Pyongyang with immediate security assurances, fuel, grain, and battlefield technologies in exchange for munitions and troops. What Russia’s sparsely populated Far East cannot provide is the industrial supply chain, consumer goods, agricultural inputs, and commercial scale that keep the North Korean economy functioning.
The “Russia card” certainly gave Kim the breathing room to negotiate with Beijing from a position of confidence rather than desperation. In the end, though, geography and scale bring Pyongyang back to the Yalu. By opening the bridge five weeks after the Tumen crossing, Beijing is reminding both Pyongyang and the world where the Peninsula’s real economic lifeline lies.
Once Beijing accepted a nuclear-armed North Korea as a baseline reality, keeping its primary commercial artery padlocked no longer made strategic sense.
NO THREE-WAY MILITARY PACT
The second misconception is that twin bridge openings with Russia and China within five weeks prove that a formal, monolithic Beijing-Moscow-Pyongyang bloc has locked into place. In reality, Beijing is moving to protect its bilateral leverage precisely because its horizon differs from Moscow’s.
Russia and North Korea are currently bound by urgent, transactional wartime needs, making both capitals comfortable with visible geopolitical disruption. Beijing’s priorities are fundamentally different.
As a global trading power deeply integrated into international markets, China wants a stable buffer state in Pyongyang and a resilient partner in Moscow, but it prefers to manage its relations with both on separate bilateral tracks rather than appearing to endorse a formal trilateral axis that could invite secondary sanctions or harden allied counter-coalitions.
Revitalising Liaoning province – for which Dandong is the commercial gateway – and anchoring North Korea inside China’s economic orbit achieves Beijing’s goals without the diplomatic costs of a three-way military pact.
Finally, the bridge’s opening carries a stark message for Washington and Seoul. With US President Donald Trump having already acknowledged North Korea’s “57” nuclear weapons as a practical reality while hinting at a return to leader-level diplomacy, the traditional bargain of trading sanctions relief for denuclearisation is obsolete.
Physical infrastructure is destiny. A nuclear-armed North Korea connected by a four-lane highway to China’s industrial heartland and a new road link to Russia is insulated against economic coercion as never before.
If Washington returns to the negotiating table with Pyongyang, it will find that the economic leverage it once hoped to trade away has already been paved over across the Yalu.
Seong-Hyon Lee, PhD, is a senior fellow at the George HW Bush Foundation for US-China Relations and an associate-in-research at the Harvard University Asia Centre. This commentary first appeared on Lowy Institute’s blog, The Interpreter.

articles.summary: Hong Kong, ASEAN can ‘drive economic cooperation across APEC’  Asia News Network
articles.full_text:
HONG KONG – The 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Finance Ministerial Meeting, which began in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region on Tuesday, offers a platform for strengthening economic cooperation among the grouping’s 21 member economies, experts said.
And, with Hong Kong and most of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations economies being APEC members, they can utilize this valuable opportunity to discuss how to step up economic cooperation.
Hong Kong itself can play a very important complementary role in supporting the supply-chain restructuring process in the 11-member ASEAN grouping by providing a host of professional services, economists told China Daily.
Backed by Asia’s strong inter-regional trade due to market diversification and deeper trade ties, International Monetary Fund projects in Asia would contribute two-thirds of the world’s economic growth in the next few years.
The ASEAN economies, in particular, have been driven by a technology boom and strong growth in exports of semiconductors and artificial intelligence infrastructure.
“The rise of technology has provided a sizeable boost to several major Asian economies, with exports growth having risen sharply in the first half of this year. This was driven by technology products, strong demand for AI infrastructure, and investment in data centers,” said IMF Asia and Pacific Department Director, Krishna Srinivasan.
Asia’s exports strength extends beyond the technology boom, with trade performing better than expected despite tariffs, including non-technology exports. This was supported by the diversification of export markets, robust intra-regional trade and more trade agreements.
“Growth, surprisingly, has been stronger in India, while South Korea and some ASEAN economies have seen significant growth on the back of the technology boom,” Srinivasan said.
Besides strong exports, another economic transformation driver for the ASEAN economies is supply-chain restructuring.
The China Plus One (C+1) strategy is a business and supply-chain approach with companies maintaining operations in China while establishing production or sourcing capacity in at least one other country to diversify risk and reduce dependency.
As this strategy is becoming less effective due to widespread tariffs imposed by the United States, many countries are shifting to hedging strategies, localizing production and exploring domestic markets. As a result, after experiencing strong export growth, ASEAN economies are now demanding professional services to facilitate supply-chain restructuring.
Tang Hei-wai — associate vice-president (global) and director at The University of Hong Kong’s Asia Global Institute — said Southeast Asia has benefited greatly from supply-chain restructuring with the signing of trade pacts under the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, robust infrastructure, and openness to foreign direct investment.
He said Hong Kong, as a financial and professional services hub, can support the ASEAN economies in supply-chain restructuring through trade finance and insurance.
“For Hong Kong to be a member of the RCEP, it can help some of the grouping’s economies overcome some of the challenges in supply-chain restructuring, especially when it comes to financial support and offering professional services, such as insurance, and supply-chain management,” Tang told China Daily.
Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said besides ASEAN, Middle Eastern and Central Asian countries can also leverage Hong Kong’s professional services in promoting economic growth.
“As Middle Eastern and Central Asian economies continue to develop and diversify, the SAR can support their economic growth by mobilizing long-term capital, broadening currency options, and managing and sharing risks,” Chan said.
The finance chief said international multilateral organizations, financial institutions and insurers can cooperate by using innovative methods to promote more efficient capital mobilization and risk management.
“With Hong Kong’s concentration of relevant professional expertise, abundant capital and extensive experience, the city can help structure projects to make them bankable, fostering a virtuous cycle in driving growth and investment opportunities,” he said.

KIDF delegation engages investors and financial institutions during the Milken Institute Asia Summit.
A delegation from the Kazakhstan Investment Development Fund (KIDF) participated in the 13th Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore from 7 to 9 October 2026 to explore investment opportunities and develop partnerships with international investors. Supported by the Embassy of Kazakhstan in Singapore, the delegation engaged with financial institutions, investment funds and companies to discuss foreign direct investment and co-investment opportunities in Kazakhstan.
The delegation was led by Mr. Zhussup Yeralin, Chairman of the Management Board of KIDF, and included Mr. Turar Baissarinov, Deputy Chairman of the Management Board, and Mr. Aidyn Sadykzhan, Director of the Partnerships Department.
During the summit, Mr. Yeralin participated as a speaker in a session entitled “The Eurasian Economic Corridor: The New Geography of Global Trade Connectivity”. The discussion addressed emerging trade routes, regional connectivity and Eurasia’s role in global economic integration.
The delegation also held engagements with international investors, financial institutions, investment funds and leading companies based in Singapore. These discussions focused on attracting foreign direct investment into Kazakhstan, developing co-investment mechanisms and establishing long-term strategic partnerships in priority sectors of the country’s economy.
KIDF serves as an investment platform supporting major projects in Kazakhstan. It offers foreign partners opportunities for co-investment and minority equity participation, alongside assistance in navigating the country’s local investment environment. Through these arrangements, the fund facilitates engagement between international investors and investment projects in Kazakhstan.
The 13th Milken Institute Asia Summit was organised by the Milken Institute, a United States-based non-profit, non-partisan think tank focused on advancing innovative solutions to economic, financial and social challenges. The summit provided a platform for discussions on global economic developments, investment and trade connectivity.
The Embassy of Kazakhstan in Singapore supported the delegation’s participation and continued its work to facilitate investment dialogue between Kazakhstan and potential international partners. Its efforts included connecting prospective investors and promoting awareness of Kazakhstan’s investment opportunities and its position as a gateway to Central Asia.
The delegation’s participation reflected Kazakhstan’s engagement with Singapore-based investors and financial institutions to explore potential investment partnerships and support the development of economic ties between the two countries.

articles.title: Vietnam faces billions of USD in investment: An opportunity for businesses to create real value. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Vietnam faces billions of USD in investment: An opportunity for businesses to create real value.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Being upgraded by FTSE Russell opens up opportunities to access international capital flows, but also requires businesses to improve governance quality, information transparency, and the ability to generate sustainable cash flow.
Within the framework of Coteccons' 2026 Annual General Meeting of Shareholders on October 20th, a discussion session titled "The Window of Opportunity - Vietnam's Capital Market" was held, moderated by Mr. Bolat Duisenov, Chairman of the Board of Directors of Coteccons, along with speakers Nguyen Quang Thuan, Founder and Chairman of FiinGroup, and Mr. Johan Nyvene, Chairman of HSC.
An upgrade in market status does not mean that foreign capital will immediately flow into Vietnam.
According to Bolat Duisenov, Vietnam's upgrade by FTSE Russell is a significant milestone, reflecting the economy 's increasingly prominent position on the global investment map. However, this is only the beginning and does not guarantee the automatic movement of capital.
"In construction, project approval doesn't automatically guarantee success. The same applies to the capital market; an upgrade in market status doesn't automatically mean capital will flow in. Opportunities have opened up, but capital always has the right to choose," said Bolat Duisenov.
In reality, despite Vietnam's upgrade in status, foreign investors still tend to be net sellers, and market liquidity has not shown improvement commensurate with expectations.
Johan Nyvene explained that the global stock market is experiencing an unusual phase compared to before, with cautious and volatile investment sentiment. Upgrading the market status is a process, not a "magic spell" that will instantly make Vietnam a destination for foreign investors. Funds can disburse funds in stages, but they are not obligated to do so if market conditions are unfavorable.
Sharing the same view, Mr. Nguyen Quang Thuan believes that high USD interest rates, with US government bond yields above 5%, are putting pressure on capital flows into other markets. Some funds in Vietnam that have already made profits may take profits and withdraw their funds back to the US. Upgrading the rating is a necessary condition, but not a sufficient one. Institutional investors will continue to assess the quality of businesses, asset quality, and cash flow generation capabilities before deciding on capital allocation.
Another barrier mentioned by the speakers was the limit on foreign ownership in certain businesses. Therefore, considering relaxing foreign ownership limits in appropriate sectors could help expand opportunities for international investors to participate.
Mr. Johan Nyvene also noted that the structure of the Vietnamese stock market currently has a large proportion of capital concentrated in the banking, securities, and real estate sectors. Meanwhile, international capital flows are paying more attention to technology and artificial intelligence. The lack of technology companies with international scale and competitiveness is also a factor that makes the Vietnamese market not yet attractive enough for global capital flows.
The quality of governance and the ability to execute decisions determine a company's attractiveness.
You may also like
From the topic of capital markets, the discussion shifted to a more specific issue: What changes do Vietnamese businesses, or more specifically Coteccons, need to make to become attractive destinations for investors?
According to Mr. Nguyen Quang Thuan, institutional investors are usually primarily interested in the growth prospects of the industry and the enterprise. This is assessed particularly through the competitive position, quality of governance, and resilience of the enterprise in the face of difficult periods. The concern of foreign investors is entrusting multi-billion dollar projects to contractors without knowing whether the enterprise can survive.
Given that the market may continue to face difficulties in the next 2-3 years, Coteccons needs to be more selective about its clients, diversify its business areas, and strengthen its approach to FDI clients.
Furthermore, FDI enterprises often pay higher prices, but also set stringent standards regarding quality, timelines, governance, and sustainable development. From this perspective, ESG is considered one of the foundations that helps businesses identify risks early, use resources efficiently, increase transparency, and strengthen trust with employees, customers, partners, investors, and the community.
Coteccons has made positive strides in the field of ESG. In the future, Coteccons needs to explore new areas of activity. While revenue growth was previously the primary metric, today institutional investors focus more on governance quality, capital efficiency, risk management capabilities, ESG, and the ability to generate sustainable cash flow.
Therefore, to build trust with investors, businesses need to maintain strict governance discipline, control risks, and prepare sufficient financial capacity to weather unfavorable cycles.
From Coteccons' perspective, Mr. Bolat Duisenov believes that this is the time for the market to shift from a growth-at-all-costs mindset to "Quality Growth." The ultimate measure of a business lies in its ability to transform workload into tangible business results, value for customers, and profits for shareholders.
The need for trillions of USD in capital necessitates the development of the capital market.
Another topic that speakers focused on discussing was Vietnam's ability to meet its capital needs during the 2026-2030 period.
Mr. Johan Nyvene shared that Vietnam's challenge lies not only in attracting capital flows, but also in its ability to form and develop long-term capital sources. Currently, bank credit remains the primary source of capital for businesses.
In reality, not many businesses are willing to spend the time and money, potentially up to six months, on a credit rating assessment, when a bank loan is often a quicker and more convenient option.
Meanwhile, Mr. Nguyen Quang Thuan estimates that Vietnam needs approximately $1.5 trillion in capital between 2026 and 2030. This requires the capital market to develop accordingly, expanding fundraising channels outside the banking system.
You may also like
For Coteccons, the company needs to focus on customer selection, especially given the challenging outlook for the residential real estate market in the coming year. Diversifying into FDI clients, while also participating in infrastructure projects such as bridges, roads, and airports, could open up further growth potential.
Concluding the discussion, Mr. Bolat Duisenov emphasized that businesses wishing to attract investment need to build a stable foundation, sustainable execution capabilities, and strong financial health. Transparency of information is also a crucial factor in building trust with investors.
For Coteccons, the defined strategy is to continue pursuing quality growth, focusing on selecting suitable clients, managing risks, improving productivity, ensuring construction quality, and transforming backlog into profits and sustainable cash flow.
Vietnam possesses attractive development opportunities in the region, but capital flows will not necessarily seek out the largest or fastest-growing businesses, but rather prioritize those with high credibility.
“Coteccons believes that quality growth is the foundation for building Trust Capital. This is not only market capital but also the trust of customers, shareholders, partners, and employees,” said Mr. Bolat Duisenov.

articles.title: After the Bangkok Blueprint, Can ASEAN’s Financial Systems Still Fail Separately? - Modern Diplomacy
articles.summary: After the Bangkok Blueprint, Can ASEAN’s Financial Systems Still Fail Separately?  Modern Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
The Bangkok Blueprint calls for cooperation against cross-border financial fraud. As ASEAN deepens digital integration and expands its role in the global AI economy, shared technological dependencies present another risk that financial decision makers need to understand before disruption occurs.
On 14 October 2026, the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, working with the Bank of Thailand, launched the Bangkok Blueprint for Fraud-Resilient Financial Services. Its central point is that technology-enabled financial fraud crosses institutional and national boundaries, requiring coordinated responses beyond individual banks.
The Blueprint addresses fraud, not AI infrastructure concentration. Yet its approach offers a useful lesson for another vulnerability. Financial institutions operating under different regulators may depend on the same cloud platforms, AI models, or upstream technology providers. Each institution can maintain sound controls while shared dependencies remain difficult to recognize at the regional level.
The Integration Paradox
ASEAN concluded negotiations on its Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) in May 2026, ahead of its planned signing. The agreement covers electronic payments, digital identity, data governance, cybersecurity cooperation, and emerging technologies. Studies cited by ASEAN suggest the region’s digital economy could double to US$2 trillion by 2030 if the agreement is successfully implemented.
Greater interoperability promises lower transaction costs and more efficient financial services. The ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO) makes a related argument in its ASEAN+3 Financial Stability Report 2026, released on 5 October. Digital connectivity can support deeper financial integration, improving market efficiency and systemic resilience. The same report identifies high asset concentration in AI, rapid financial digitalization, and evolving financial linkages as forces reshaping the region’s risk landscape.
That exposure is visible in growth projections. In an October 2026 economic analysis, AMRO staff estimate that ASEAN+3 growth in 2027 could fall from 4.1 to 2.6 percent if US technology investment, used as a proxy for global AI demand, slows to its 2024 growth rate.
That scenario measures sensitivity to AI investment, not losses from banking technology failure. It nevertheless shows how much the AI economy now matters to regional growth, even as financial institutions adopt technologies supplied by an industry exposed to changing investment conditions.
Integration can diversify financial markets while leaving their supporting infrastructure concentrated.
What Banks May Have in Common
Banks have good reasons to rely on major technology providers. Large cloud and AI companies offer security capabilities, technical expertise, and recovery resources that individual institutions cannot easily reproduce.
Moving critical services to smaller vendors is not automatically safer. Provider quality and systemic concentration are different questions. Even a highly resilient supplier becomes a common exposure when numerous institutions depend on its services.
The Financial Stability Board (FSB) has identified third-party concentration, market correlations, and cybersecurity among AI-related financial vulnerabilities. Its 2025 monitoring report includes a case study on AI-related third-party dependencies and service provider concentration and calls for authorities to address data gaps in monitoring.
Indonesia’s Financial Services Authority, Otoritas Jasa Keuangan (OJK), has also recognized systemic third-party dependencies and correlated AI-driven behavior in its 2025 banking AI governance guidance.
Two mechanisms deserve attention. A common provider can suffer an outage, disrupting several institutions simultaneously. Alternatively, AI systems can continue operating while generating similar responses to market stress, prompting banks to tighten credit or increase liquidity buffers together. The second problem is harder to detect because nothing has technically broken. The technology may be working exactly as its users intended, even as their collective decisions amplify financial instability.
Recent incidents illustrate operational concentration risks. In July 2024, a faulty CrowdStrike software update disrupted computer systems across multiple industries. A month earlier, a ransomware attack on Indonesia’s Temporary National Data Centre disrupted public services, including immigration.
Neither incident was an AI banking failure. Both show how disruptions involving shared technology or centralized services can affect otherwise separate organizations.
No publicly available, comparable ASEAN-wide dataset appears to measure critical AI dependencies across financial institutions. This does not establish that systemic concentration already exists. It leaves policymakers without an accessible regional picture of where common exposure may be developing.
Agentic AI Changes the Speed
On 7 October 2026, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) issued its final Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management for Financial Institutions, effective from 7 October 2027. The guidelines recognize AI systems with greater autonomy in generating outputs, making decisions, and executing actions.
Agentic AI is not yet widespread across critical banking operations. Nevertheless, systems that can access tools and execute authorized workflows introduce different pressures from models that merely recommend actions.
If similar agents eventually support payments, treasury, or risk management across institutions, a common disturbance could produce financial responses before operators fully understand its origin. Actual consequences will depend on deployment and safeguards, but faster execution can reduce the time available for intervention.
Why Singapore Matters
Singapore illustrates why these risks cannot be assessed solely through national supervision.
According to the International Monetary Fund, Singapore’s banking assets reached 512 percent of GDP at the end of 2024. Claims on non-residents amounted to 116.6 per cent of GDP, equivalent to approximately 23 per cent of total banking assets.
Singapore was also the world’s third-largest foreign-exchange center, handling US$1.485 trillion in average daily trading in April 2025.
These figures demonstrate connectivity rather than institutional weakness. A prolonged disruption affecting critical payments, liquidity management, or foreign-exchange services operating through Singapore could have consequences for institutions and businesses elsewhere in ASEAN.
Geopolitics adds another concern. US export controls on advanced computing show how access to technology can be shaped by strategic decisions. Restrictions affecting suppliers need not target ASEAN directly to impose adjustment costs on regional financial institutions.
When Financial Disruption Reaches the Real Economy
According to the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development, ASEAN attracted a record US$243.9 billion in foreign direct investment in 2025. Semiconductors, electronics, and digital infrastructure are among the industries attracting strategic capital as the region expands its role in global AI supply chains.
Major projects often rely on parent-company funding or international capital markets rather than domestic bank lending. Their implementation nevertheless requires cross-border payments, foreign-exchange hedging, trade finance, and working capital for local suppliers.
A prolonged disruption affecting shared financial technology could interfere with these services across several markets. Equipment payments might be delayed, import financing constrained, or contractors forced to manage cash-flow gaps. The Basel Committee’s Principles for Operational Resilience emphasize maintaining critical banking operations and managing third-party dependencies during severe disruptions.
The concern is not that a single technology outage would derail ASEAN’s industrialization. Hidden dependencies could interrupt the financial services supporting investment execution, especially during global economic uncertainty. Discovering them during a disruption forces institutions to investigate shared exposures while restoring essential services. Identifying them beforehand allows decision makers to determine which functions deserve stronger safeguards and where additional resilience spending is justified.
Building on ASEAN’s Existing Cooperation
Europe offers a practical precedent. Under the Digital Operational Resilience Act, European authorities assess critical technology providers’ systemic importance and substitutability. In November 2025, they published their first list of designated critical providers.
ASEAN can draw on this principle without reproducing Europe’s regulatory architecture. Its financial cooperation mechanisms already provide a starting point.
The ASEAN Senior Level Committee on Financial Integration (SLC), co-chaired by Bank Indonesia and the State Bank of Vietnam during 2024–2026, receives risk-monitoring reports on macroeconomic and financial-stability risks within its working committees’ purview and on their implications for regional integration.
ASEAN also has experience in cross-border cybersecurity cooperation. In an August 2023 statement, Bank Indonesia reported an opportunity to coordinate the Cybersecurity Resilience and Information Sharing Platform (CRISP), a forum supporting cybersecurity cooperation and information exchange among ASEAN central banks.
CRISP is a precedent for sharing cyber-threat information, not an existing mechanism for mapping financial institutions’ technology providers. Such an assessment requires banking supervisors and payment-system authorities, in addition to cybersecurity specialists.

articles.title: World Bank, IMF Project Indonesia GDP Growth Above 5% on AI Demand and State Spending - InvestorTrust
articles.summary: World Bank, IMF Project Indonesia GDP Growth Above 5% on AI Demand and State Spending  InvestorTrust
articles.full_text:
JAKARTA, Investortrust.id — Indonesia’s macroeconomic expansion is set to remain firmly above the 5% mark over the medium term, with both the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projecting resilient momentum supported by the global artificial intelligence boom and sustained public spending.
The World Bank upgraded its 2026 gross domestic product (GDP) growth projection for Southeast Asia's largest economy by 0.5 percentage points to 5.2% year-on-year, while forecasting stable performance heading into 2027. Concurrently, the IMF maintained its Indonesian growth estimate at 5.1% across both 2026 and 2027.
The upgraded forecasts highlight how domestic public investments and global technological shifts are shielding Southeast Asia from external headwinds, including elevated global borrowing costs and sticky geopolitical tensions. However, with multilateral lenders warning of widening fiscal imbalances and a rising current-account deficit, Jakarta faces the challenge of weaning its economy off state-led stimulus and fostering private-sector capital investment to sustain momentum.
According to the World Bank, the broader East Asia and Pacific region is expanding at an accelerated pace, propelled by the production and export of high-technology goods essential to global artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Domestic Resilience
For Indonesia, domestic resilience was further bolstered as the negative economic fallout from elevated international energy prices proved milder than initially feared. Economic activity has also drawn substantial momentum from central government priority programs, capital expenditures linked to state-owned enterprises (SOEs), and ongoing energy subsidies.
However, the Washington-based lender cautioned that this policy mix—while effective in supporting short-term output—comes at the cost of expanding twin deficits. The World Bank projects Indonesia’s current-account deficit to widen to 1.5% of GDP in 2026.
"As fiscal stimulus wanes, medium-term growth is projected to rely increasingly on private investment," the World Bank stated in its assessment on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. "Meanwhile, inflation is expected to remain near the upper end of the central bank's target band."
Reinforcing the multilateral lenders' outlook on state-driven momentum, Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara confirmed that fourth-quarter government spending is projected to reach Rp 1,300 trillion ($81.6 billion), climbing from Rp 1,200 trillion in the final quarter of 2025.
"Food assistance has begun rolling out for the fourth quarter, which will drive household consumption and bolster government expenditure across our economy," Suahasil told reporters at the Presidential Palace complex in Jakarta on Monday. "Indonesia's macroeconomic condition and domestic transaction activity remain highly resilient. We will continue safeguarding stability while driving growth."
Easing Inflation
In a parallel assessment, the IMF projected headline domestic inflation to land at 3.3% in 2026 before easing to 2.8% in 2027.
The fund highlighted that rapid technological momentum spearheaded by AI adoption serves as an essential counterweight against international geopolitical fragmentation throughout the Asia-Pacific corridor. In the immediate term, this trend is manifesting via rising export demand, capital deepening, and direct infrastructure outlays, while broader long-term adoption holds the potential to significantly lift total factor productivity.
The IMF noted that net global trade in AI computing hardware has expanded exponentially as a share of world GDP, though the value gain has been driven primarily by premium pricing structures rather than sheer physical volume.
The fund added a note of caution, however, observing that the economic windfall from AI is unlikely to be distributed evenly across developing economies. The global AI architecture remains intensely concentrated across upstream high-performance computing hardware required for training and inference, as well as downstream enterprise frontier model development.

articles.title: Tech sector growth opens up opportunities for Việt Nam to go global - vietnamnews.vn
articles.summary: Tech sector growth opens up opportunities for Việt Nam to go global  vietnamnews.vn
articles.full_text:
| In the semiconductor industry, opportunities lie not only in chip manufacturing, but also in supporting sectors such as components, materials, precision engineering, equipment and automation. VNA/VNS Photo | 
HÀ NỘI — The growth of the electronics, semiconductor and high-tech sectors worldwide is opening up a variety of opportunities for Vietnamese enterprises to integrate more deeply into the global supply chain.
However, to become suppliers for these corporations, domestic enterprises must meet rigorous standards regarding quality, technology, productivity and order fulfilment capabilities.
Industry insiders have said that in the semiconductor sector, opportunities lie not only in chip manufacturing, but also in supporting sectors such as components, materials, precision engineering, equipment and automation.
These areas can serve as entry points for domestic enterprises to gradually integrate into the manufacturing ecosystem, gain experience and enhance their technical capabilities.
But simply possessing a factory or production line is insufficient to guarantee status as a supplier to major corporations.
Enterprises must also demonstrate their ability to control quality, maintain process stability, ensure timely delivery and meet technical standards. Within the electronics and semiconductor supply chain, even a minor quality deviation can impact the entire production process.
International buyers thus often impose rigorous requirements regarding suppliers' quality management systems, traceability and risk management capabilities.
It is thus necessary for Vietnamese enterprises to invest more systematically in technology, automation and production management systems. Rather than competing solely on labour costs, businesses need to improve productivity, reduce defect rates and enhance their capacity to fulfil orders with demanding technical specifications.
Experts suggest that a practical approach is to begin by supplying components, materials or support services to FDI enterprises operating in Việt Nam.
Such partnerships enable domestic firms to adopt international standards, refine their production processes and build a foundation for gradually participating in higher value-added stages of the industry.
Aside from technical capabilities, experts said Vietnamese enterprises should also prioritise environmental, social and governance (ESG) standards, as they are increasingly becoming a key factor in international supply chains, ranking alongside product quality, cost and delivery schedules.
Trần Thị Thu Trang, chairwoman of Hanel PT New Generation Technology JSC, said that Vietnamese enterprises have never had such a significant opportunity as they do now.
With double-digit growth targets, Việt Nam has issued Resolution 57-NQ/TW to make science, technology, innovation and digital transformation core drivers of national growth and self-reliance.
Trang said that with this golden opportunity at hand, the time to act is now. However, she noted that the country must accelerate the sector's development, as the chance is narrowing given the rapid pace of AI growth.
The selection process for suppliers is rigorous and determines which ones will move forward. During this critical phase, Trang urged enterprises to promote cooperation, as it is difficult to expand alone.
In addition, Trang also emphasised that ESG should not be viewed merely as a cost, but rather as a profitable investment and opportunity for businesses.
"Without proper risk management, the faster we grow, the greater the risk of being eliminated from the game," she noted.
Vice Chairman of the Bắc Ninh City People's Committee Phạm Văn Thịnh said that Bắc Ninh has advantages in electronics manufacturing, high-tech industries and a network of FDI enterprises. To capitalise on opportunities to join the supply chain, Vietnamese businesses must invest in technology, personnel and research and development, while strengthening connections with experts.
According to Thịnh, neither Bắc Ninh nor Việt Nam has much time left to establish itself as a major global supply hub. The opportunity may last only about five years. By 2031, the influx of large factories relocating to Việt Nam, and especially Bắc Ninh, may significantly diminish.

Chen Xi, a spokesperson for the Ministry of National Defense, made the statement on Friday in response to a media query concerning the Philippines' recent provocations near China's Huangyan Dao and Ren'ai Jiao, as well as its military's claims about Chinese vessels and China's intentions in the area.
China has indisputable sovereignty over Huangyan Dao and Nansha Qundao, including Zhongye Dao, Xianbin Jiao and Ren'ai Jiao, and their adjacent waters, and has sovereign rights and jurisdiction over relevant waters, Chen said.
These islands and reefs lie outside Philippine territory. Meanwhile, the Chinese side is taking necessary measures in accordance with relevant laws and regulations to uphold its sovereign rights, which are legitimate, reasonable, professional and standardized, the spokesperson said.
For some time, the Philippine side has been rallying external forces to stir up trouble in the South China Sea, while violating others' sovereignty, making provocations and distorting facts to spread false narratives. All these have made the Philippines a destroyer of peace and a destabilizing factor in the South China Sea, Chen said.
In response to another media query, the spokesperson slammed Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro's hyping of the South China Sea issue and his false remarks about China.
"A certain Philippine politician cares only about his selfish interests, trying to gain political influence by taking an extreme anti-China position, expand his own military power by creating 'external threats,' and trade for foreign support through stirring up trouble in the South China Sea," Chen said.

 On October 20th, the Ho Chi Minh City Trade and Investment Promotion Center (ITPC), in collaboration with the Ho Chi Minh City Mechanical and Electrical Business Association (HAMEE), inaugurated the "2026 Business Networking and Product Introduction Week for the Mechanical, Electrical, and Digital Technology Industries".
 The program is organized according to Plan No. 136/KH-UBND of the People's Committee of Ho Chi Minh City, aiming to support businesses in promoting products, connecting with partners, expanding markets, and enhancing competitiveness in the field of mechanical engineering and automation.
 According to Mr. Le Anh Hoang, Deputy Director of ITPC, the period from 2026 to 2030 is a time when Ho Chi Minh City will accelerate the innovation of its growth model, taking "dual transformation" including digitalization and greening as core driving forces. The city aims for the digital economy to contribute 30-40% of GRDP and the green economy to reach at least 10% of GRDP by 2030.
 To realize these goals, the mechanical and electrical engineering sectors play a crucial role in providing equipment, automation solutions, and technology for modern production. The application of digital technology and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) standards not only helps businesses improve productivity but also enables them to meet the requirements of multinational corporations.
 The potential for growth in this sector is demonstrated by the country's export results. According to the Customs Department, in the first eight months of 2026, the export value of computers, electronic products, and components reached US$101.06 billion, an increase of 51.1% compared to the same period last year. This is the first time this product group has surpassed the US$100 billion mark in just eight months, continuing to hold the leading position in export value. In the same period last year, the machinery, equipment, tools, and spare parts group reached nearly US$47.3 billion, an increase of 26.4%.
 The growth rate of these two product groups indicates a strong demand for manufactured and technological products. However, opportunities from the export market can only translate into higher added value for domestic businesses when supply capacity, product quality, and localization rates are improved. This is also why Ho Chi Minh City aims to raise the localization rate to over 30% by 2030.
 To get closer to this goal, mechanical and electrical engineering businesses need to overcome limitations in capital, technology, ability to meet technical standards, and connections with major manufacturers.
 Against this backdrop, this year's business networking week brings together 22 leading enterprises, showcasing products and solutions across five sectors: mechanical engineering, supporting industries, construction machinery, electrical equipment - digital technology, and raw materials and supplies. This event is expected to create more opportunities for cooperation between businesses in the production chain, from component supply to the development of complete equipment and systems.
 Mr. Tran Thanh Trong, a member of the Ho Chi Minh City People's Council and First Vice Chairman of HAMEE, believes that manufacturing capacity and product quality only truly realize their value when businesses reach the right customers and meet the right market needs.
 According to Mr. Trong, the highlight of the program is strengthening the linkages between the three fields of mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, and digital technology. Cooperation between machine manufacturing companies and providers of control, automation, and digital technology solutions can create synchronized equipment and systems that meet the increasingly high technical demands of the market.
 HAMEE representatives expect the exhibition to translate into concrete collaborative results such as exchanging technical documents, sending samples, providing quotations, conducting factory surveys, and ultimately signing contracts. This is a necessary step for domestic businesses to enhance their ability to participate in the supply chains of large corporations.
 Besides production linkages, green transformation is an inseparable requirement for the goal of enhancing competitiveness. According to HAMEE, businesses need to start with measurable solutions such as saving electricity, reducing material waste, minimizing scrap, and optimizing equipment productivity. This process needs to be supported by technology, preferential capital, and appropriate policies.

articles.summary: MAS Warns of Financial Stability Risks as Billions Pour Into AI  Fintech Singapore

Businesses are adopting AI rapidly, but the technology has yet to deliver widespread productivity gains, according to the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).
Edward S. Robinson, MAS Deputy Managing Director (Economic Policy) and Chief Economist, highlighted this gap at the 2026 Beijing Financial Street Forum on 20 October.
AI-driven electronics account for more than 70 percent of Asia’s export growth this year.
Much of the growth in AI-producing industries reflects higher investment and equipment use rather than sustained productivity improvements.
Robinson noted that broader gains would require businesses to adapt their operations and invest in skills and infrastructure.
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) estimates that AI could boost annual productivity growth by up to 0.6 percentage points with widespread adoption and supporting investment.
AI Investment Boom Raises Financial Stability Concerns
Robinson cautioned that expectations of future AI gains could inflate asset prices and encourage excessive borrowing.
A reassessment of those expectations could trigger falling valuations and tighter credit conditions.
He stressed that central banks should base monetary policy decisions on actual economic conditions rather than anticipated productivity gains.
Monetary policy may need to remain restrictive while investment-driven demand dominates, with scope for easing once sustained productivity improvements emerge.
Robinson also called for safeguards against excessive borrowing and regulatory measures to support AI adoption.
