Vietnam has signed a free trade agreement with the four member states of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) after over 14 years of negotiation, seeking to expand trade, attract investment, and deepen economic cooperation with developed European economies.
The Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement (VEFTA) was signed in Hanoi on Sunday in the presence of Vietnamese Party Chief and President To Lam and representatives of the participating countries.
The deal is Vietnam’s 18th free trade agreement (FTA) with foreign countries and trading blocs.
EFTA is an intergovernmental organization comprising Switzerland, Iceland, Norway and Liechtenstein, with strengths in innovation and advanced industries. The agreement aims to strengthen economic ties, promote free trade, and reinforce a rules-based trading system amid global economic uncertainty.
VEFTA covers trade in goods, including tariffs, technical barriers, customs procedures and trade remedies, as well as services, investment, intellectual property, dispute settlement, trade and sustainable development.
For Vietnam, the agreement is expected to diversify export and import markets, improve business competitiveness, and help domestic companies integrate more deeply into global value chains.
It could also create opportunities to attract higher-quality investment, advanced technology and management expertise from developed European economies.
According to the Ministry of Industry and Trade, annual trade between Vietnam and EFTA members currently averages around $2 billion. Vietnam mainly exports seafood, footwear, textiles and garments and electronic equipment to the bloc, while importing machinery, industrial equipment, chemicals and pharmaceuticals.
As of the end of 2025, Switzerland had 234 valid projects in Vietnam, with registered investment of $2.4 billion. Norway had 62 projects with registered capital of over $200 million.
Swiss President Guy Parmelin welcomed the signing of VEFTA during a meeting with Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung in Hanoi last Saturday, held as part of his official visit to Vietnam.
Parmelin said the agreement would create opportunities to expand trade and investment and strengthen business links between the two countries, particularly among small and medium-sized enterprises.
Switzerland is ready to share its expertise and strengths in insurance, reinsurance, manufacturing, precision machinery and high technology, he stressed.The Swiss president also proposed linking Switzerland’s Crypto Valley hub with Vietnam’s innovation ecosystem to promote cooperation in blockchain, artificial intelligence and quantum technology.

articles.title: Indonesia’s Oil Import Bill Jumps 40% as Fuel Subsidies Shield Households - Sri Lanka Guardian
articles.summary: Indonesia’s Oil Import Bill Jumps 40% as Fuel Subsidies Shield Households  Sri Lanka Guardian
articles.full_text:
Indonesia’s oil and gas import bill surged 40.2 per cent year on year to US$25.8 billion in the first seven months of 2026, as higher global energy prices increased pressure on the country’s public finances and external accounts. Government subsidies have shielded households from much of the price shock, but the cost of keeping domestic energy affordable has risen sharply.
An analysis by The Business Times of Statistics Indonesia data found that the increase in import expenditure far outpaced the 10.9 per cent rise in physical import volumes. The country’s oil and gas trade deficit consequently widened 78.2 per cent to US$18.8 billion over the same period.
Economists say Indonesia has several buffers against the shock, including government subsidies and earnings from commodity exports. Higher coal and palm oil prices have helped offset some of the pressure from more expensive oil imports, although the government has had to absorb a growing share of the additional energy costs.
Subsidies and compensation payments reached 331.4 trillion rupiah (US$18.4 billion) through August, an increase of 52.1 per cent from a year earlier, as the government limited the impact of rising international prices on consumers.
Data from Bank Indonesia (BI) showed that the pressure intensified in the second quarter. The value of oil imports climbed to US$11.6 billion from US$7.3 billion in the first quarter, even as import volumes declined to 88 million barrels from 90 million. Spending on refined petroleum products rose to US$7.8 billion from US$4.4 billion, while volumes increased more modestly to 57 million barrels from 54 million.
BI attributed the higher import bill to rising international oil prices following the outbreak of conflict in the Middle East on 28 February. Brent crude climbed from US$72.48 a barrel on 27 February to a peak of about US$126 in April. It was trading at around US$107.31 on 19 October, approximately 48 per cent above its pre-conflict level, according to Bloomberg data.
The energy shock has also affected Indonesia’s external accounts. The current-account deficit widened to US$12.5 billion, equivalent to 3.3 per cent of gross domestic product, in the second quarter, from US$3.6 billion, or 1 per cent of GDP, in the first three months of the year. BI attributed the deterioration partly to higher oil imports, alongside stronger non-oil imports and larger services and income deficits.
However, Maybank Securities economist Brian Lee said the impact was “more significant for the fiscal position than for the external accounts”, noting that Indonesia remained a major commodity exporter. Higher coal and palm oil prices, he said, were benefiting two of the country’s largest export categories as alternative energy feedstocks became more valuable. Lee expects the current-account deficit to average 2 per cent of GDP in 2026.
For households, fuel subsidies and administrative measures have limited direct increases in domestic fuel and energy prices. OCBC senior Asean economist Lavanya Venkateswaran said this had shifted the burden towards public finances, the exchange rate and the balance of payments.
The increase in subsidy spending has also exceeded the growth in subsidised consumption. Volumes of subsidised fuel rose 8.8 per cent, while consumption of subsidised three-kilogram liquefied petroleum gas cylinders, widely used for household cooking, increased 2.6 per cent.
The government has incorporated higher energy costs and a weaker currency into its 2027 Budget assumptions, using an Indonesian crude price of US$75 a barrel and an exchange rate of 17,500 rupiah to the US dollar, compared with US$70 and 16,500 rupiah in the 2026 Budget. The Finance Ministry’s September update put this year’s average Indonesian crude price at US$89.20 a barrel and the average exchange rate at 17,415 rupiah per US dollar.
Lee cautioned that the revised assumptions could still prove optimistic if current conditions persisted. Nevertheless, he said Indonesia retained “meaningful buffers”, with the 2027 fiscal deficit target of 2.4 per cent of GDP remaining below the statutory ceiling of 3 per cent.
The currency and inflation pressures could complicate monetary policy even as subsidies restrain retail energy prices. BI has raised interest rates three times this year by a combined 100 basis points, bringing its benchmark rate to 5.75 per cent. OCBC expects one further increase of 25 basis points in 2026, while forecasting economic growth of 5.2 per cent this year and 5 per cent in 2027.
Venkateswaran said the main warning sign would be “a simultaneous deterioration across external accounts, fiscal metrics, and market confidence”, adding: “This is not our base case.”

articles.title: China's economy: Record-high trade surplus, real estate market shows no signs of bottoming out. - Vietnam.vn

articles.full_text:
|  | 
| Investment continues to be a weakness of the Chinese economy. (Source: Getty Images) | 
 According to data released on October 19, China's third-quarter 2026 growth rate exceeded the 4.4% forecast by economists surveyed by Reuters , and surpassed the 4.3% growth rate in the second quarter of 2026 – the lowest in three years.
 The growth momentum stems from three factors.
 Tianchen Xu, a senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit, noted that the recovery in September 2026 partially offset the less positive results in July and August.
 According to him, this improvement stems from government investment, which helped prevent a prolonged decline in fixed asset investment, along with strong export performance and a low comparative base.
 In addition, China's monthly trade surplus reached a record high of $133.5 billion.
 Mr. Xu believes that the momentum from these three factors could continue into the fourth quarter of 2026, and forecasts China's economic growth for the whole year to reach 4.7%.
 Data shows that the world's second-largest economy remains dependent on manufacturing and demand from overseas markets, while households and private investors continue to be cautious. Overall, China's economic growth averaged 4.6% in the first nine months of the year, within Beijing's official target range of 4.5-5%.
 In September 2026, retail sales increased by 1.1% year-on-year, exceeding analysts' forecasts of a 0.6% increase. Industrial production rose by 5.5%, in line with forecasts. The urban unemployment rate stood at 5.2% this month.
 However, investment continues to be a weakness of the economy. In the first nine months of the year, fixed asset investment in urban areas fell 7.2% year-on-year, lower than the 7.3% decline economists had forecast in a Reuters survey.
 Notably, investment in real estate development decreased by 20.6% in the period from January to September, a deeper decline than the 19.9% drop recorded in the first eight months of the year.
 Sheana Yue, a senior economist at Oxford Economics, argues that the prolonged downturn in the housing market will continue to limit the spillover effects from industrial activity across the economy. This is happening as Chinese households have seen their accumulated real estate holdings shrink in recent years.
 Ms. Yue also rejected the notion that the real estate market has shown clear signs of recovery. According to her, there is no basis to conclude that the Chinese real estate market has "hit rock bottom," as home sales, the number of projects started, and price trends still do not show clear signs of recovery.
 Growth relies heavily on exports.
 This year, China has relied heavily on exports to drive growth. However, this impetus is facing increasing pressure as energy costs rise sharply, while China's increased production and exports are raising concerns among its trading partners.
 Meanwhile, other sectors of the economy remain weak due to sluggish consumption and a continued decline in the real estate market after years of decline.
 Professor Eswar Prasad, an economics professor at Cornell University, assesses that the imbalance between domestic supply and demand in the world's second-largest economy continues to widen.
 According to him, the government could become more optimistic and continue its passive approach, instead of introducing further stimulus measures to the economy alongside necessary reforms.
 Pressure is also evident in price movements. Producer prices in China rose 5% in September, the fastest increase in more than four years. Meanwhile, consumer inflation remains below 1%, reflecting persistent overcapacity and weak demand, limiting businesses' ability to raise prices.
 "This could force companies to absorb much of the cost shock by accepting lower profit margins, rather than raising product prices," Yue stated.
 Economists generally predict that the People's Bank of China will keep its benchmark lending rate unchanged for the remainder of the year, meaning that fiscal measures will continue to play a major role in supporting the economy.
 While positive growth rates may ease immediate pressure on Beijing to increase stimulus, Ms. Yue expects that the implementation of announced measures will be accelerated, thereby supporting investment and economic activity in the coming quarters.

articles.title: Vietnam’s Growth Ambitions Are Outrunning Its Capital - fulcrum.sg

Vietnam’s Growth Ambitions Are Outrunning Its Capital
Published
Vietnam’s ambitious GDP growth target is premised on the building of infrastructure. But it is struggling to mobilise sufficient capital to finance such a goal.
Since coming to power in August 2024, General Secretary To Lam has emphasised his ambition to turn Vietnam into a high-income country by 2045. Towards this goal, an April 2026 National Assembly resolution set a target of average annual growth of 10 per cent through 2030, with the building of infrastructure expected to serve as a major growth engine. However, Vietnam is struggling to mobilise sufficient capital to finance this ambitious agenda because of both domestic and external constraints. Hanoi therefore faces a choice: align its growth targets with the capital it can raise at reasonable cost or accept considerably greater economic risks.
The projects illustrate the scale of the challenge. The North–South high-speed railway is projected to cost USD67 billion, while the two Ninh Thuan nuclear power plants, with a combined capacity of 4,000 megawatts (MW), are expected to cost at least USD22 billion. Financing Vietnam’s high-growth plans for 2026–2030 is estimated to require around USD297 billion annually, or about 40 per cent of nominal GDP.
Domestic banks carry most of this burden. Bank lending accounts for about 83 per cent of Vietnam’s financing mix, compared with 13 per cent for bonds and 4 per cent for equity. By late June, outstanding credit reached VND19,970 trillion (USD760 billion), up 18.1 per cent year on year. Credit expanded by 7.41 per cent in the first half, while deposits grew by only 5.02 per cent, pushing the loan-to-deposit ratio to around 111–112 per cent. Banks have responded by competing more aggressively for funding. Posted six- to twelve-month deposit rates are generally 5.0–6.5 per cent, in line with the State Bank of Vietnam’s efforts to keep rates low. In practice, however, depositors are reportedly offered effective yields of 8.5–11.0 per cent through private negotiations.
Scarce credit is also distributed unevenly. In June 2026, 18 major projects requiring VND752 trillion (USD29 billion) were exempted from standard credit-growth limits. Developers include large and well-connected conglomerates like Vingroup, Sun Group and Masterise. By contrast, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which account for 98 per cent of Vietnamese firms, receive only about 20 per cent of bank credit. They face lending rates of 10–12 per cent, while 93.5 per cent of loans require collateral. Yet SMEs account for most employment and household incomes.
The strain is already visible: new business registrations fell 13.9 per cent year on year in July, while completed dissolutions rose by 270 per cent. During a recent field trip to Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, this author repeatedly heard from businesspeople and analysts that many SMEs are struggling as they cannot access the credit needed to sustain or expand operations. This is happening despite stellar headline GDP growth of 9 per cent in the first nine months of 2026.
Vietnam can still build the roads, railways, airports and energy infrastructure it needs, but not necessarily at the pace envisaged.
High interest rates have brought the property market close to a standstill. Average home-loan rates have reached 14–16 per cent, while the number of residential property transactions nationwide fell by 36 per cent year on year in the first half. This has cooled speculation and reduced the risk of a property bubble. At the same time, however, the high rates have created new vulnerabilities. Developers depend heavily on property sales for cash flow, while their average bond issuance rate has risen to 11.4 per cent, and their debt-to-equity ratio has climbed to 74 per cent, against an average of 54 per cent during 2022–2025. Disrupted cash flows increase the risk that repayment difficulties will translate into higher bank bad debt. As China’s experience illustrates, a prolonged property slowdown can also weigh on household confidence, consumption, public finance and economic performance.
The logical response is to look abroad, but external options remain limited. The international financial centres in Da Nang and Ho Chi Minh City, launched in January and February 2026, have issued certificates to only a few dozen investors, while credit-rating requirements exclude some major foreign banks. Sovereign bond issuance is constrained by Vietnam’s credit rating, which is rated one notch below investment grade by S&P and Fitch and two by Moody’s. The government aims to achieve investment-grade status by 2030, which analysts estimate could cut borrowing costs by as much as 1.5 percentage points. But that benefit would come too late for many projects beginning now.
International capital markets are also becoming less welcoming to Vietnamese firms and banks. The US ten-year Treasury yield is around 5 per cent, while the Federal Reserve raised its target range to 3.75–4.00 per cent in September. Surging global demand for capital, particularly to finance AI and related technologies, is intensifying competition for funding. Meanwhile, geopolitical pressures, including the US-led war against Iran and the war between Ukraine and Russia, are pushing up the risk premium that emerging markets like Vietnam must pay.
Looking Ahead
There are three key implications here. First, Vietnam may need to bring its growth ambitions in line with what it can finance at reasonable cost. Moderating the growth target would ease funding pressures and put expansion on a more sustainable footing.
Second, if Hanoi maintains its targets while domestic interest rates remain high, the wider economy will bear the strain, with SMEs likely to feel it first. High borrowing costs could produce more closures and discourage private investment, leaving the economy more fragile even as infrastructure spending sustains headline GDP growth.
Third, Vietnam will increasingly need international funding, creating opportunities for foreign banks and other credit institutions. But greater reliance on debt carries risks. Much public infrastructure does not generate direct returns sufficient to service the borrowing used to fund it. In an environment of prolonged high interest rates, excessive debt-financed investment could weaken the repayment capacity of both the government and Vietnamese enterprises.
Vietnam can still build the roads, railways, airports and energy infrastructure it needs, but not necessarily at the pace envisaged. Ambition must be matched by affordable capital, and the two are increasingly moving apart. A more calibrated growth target would reduce financing pressures and the risk of a costlier debt adjustment later.

ARAU: The haze affecting Malaysia is expected to gradually improve by the end of this month as the country enters the monsoon transition phase, which could bring more rain and changes in wind direction and speed.
Universiti Malaysia Perlis (Unimap) Faculty of Civil Engineering and Technology associate professor Dr Norazian Mohamed Noor said these factors could help reduce atmospheric pollutant concentrations and limit the cross-border movement of smoke from Indonesia.
She said the Malaysian Meteorological Department's (MetMalaysia) long-range weather outlook for October to March 2027 indicated that most parts of the country were expected to receive rainfall close to their climatological averages from this month until December.
Selangor, for example, was forecast to receive between 220mm and 330mm of rain this month, and between 250mm and 380mm in November.
Kuala Lumpur, meanwhile, was expected to receive between 240mm and 360mm of rain in October, rising to between 300mm and 450mm in November.
What To Read Next
"These conditions offer a positive indication that increased rainfall could help improve air quality in Malaysia. However, the recovery may not occur simultaneously across all areas.
"Haze conditions are influenced not only by rainfall in Malaysia but also by fire activity, rainfall distribution in pollution-source areas and wind direction.
"Rainfall in our country alone is insufficient to ensure an end to transboundary haze if fires remain active at their source in Indonesia," she said recently.
Norazian said an analysis by Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency (BMKG), dated Oct 13, indicated that parts of southern Sumatra, West Kalimantan, Central Kalimantan and South Kalimantan were still expected to receive low rainfall of less than 50mm over certain 10-day periods this month.
She said the conditions could increase the risk of forest and peatland fires, particularly in areas experiencing prolonged dry spells.
"However, the BMKG forecast also indicated increased rainfall in several parts of Sumatra and Kalimantan in November and December, with some areas potentially receiving more than 300mm of rain a month.
"Should the rainfall be continuous and cover fire-affected areas, it could help reduce fire activity and smoke emissions," she said.

articles.summary: Indonesian President Prabowo marks 2 years in office with economic gains, but challenges loom  CNAPrabowo Government Gets Poor Ratings from 66% of Surveyed Professionals  Jakarta GlobeTwo years of Prabowo: Resilience today, bills tomorrow  The Jakarta PostPrabowo tightens grip on power as public support falls in Indonesia  The StarUnpacking Indonesia With Marcus Tantau  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
articles.full_text:
As Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto enters his third year in office, observers say the challenge will be to translate his ambitious promises into tangible results while balancing public expectations with economic and political stability.
DEPOK, Indonesia: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto marked two years in office on Tuesday (Oct 20), with his administration touting progress on food security and energy independence, even as questions mount over the sustainability of his ambitious social welfare programmes.
Since taking office in October 2024, Mr Prabowo has made sweeping promises to improve the lives of ordinary Indonesians, with his administration highlighting rice self-sufficiency, progress towards greater energy independence and stronger-than-expected economic growth as key achievements.
But as he enters his third year in office, the former military general faces a challenge to deliver lasting benefits without undermining Indonesia's fiscal stability.
Political manoeuvring is also expected to intensify ahead of the 2029 general election, potentially testing the durability of his broad ruling coalition.
AMBITIOUS WELFARE PLANS COME AT A COST
Among the latest proposals being considered by the government is the abolition of tuition fees at state universities nationwide.
Last month, Mr Prabowo instructed the Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Technology to develop a framework for providing free education at public universities.
Some students believe greater access to higher education deserves greater priority in the national budget.
“Spending on other programmes … such as the president’s flagship free meals programme … is much higher. I believe education should also be a priority when it comes to how our government spends its revenue,” said Isyana Balqis, an undergraduate at the University of Indonesia.
Her fellow schoolmate Amanda Putri Dimas said: “I have to work while studying to cover my tuition and other expenses. If Indonesia truly wants to achieve its Golden Indonesia vision, this should have been planned from the very beginning. I hope this plan will actually become a reality.”
The Golden Indonesia 2045 vision aims to transform the country into an advanced economy by the centenary of its independence, with education seen as key to developing a more skilled workforce.
However, the proposal comes with a substantial price tag.
The government estimates that eliminating tuition fees for nearly 3 million undergraduate and diploma students at state universities would require an additional 93 trillion rupiah (US$5 billion) annually, roughly US$1,850 per student.
While the plan has generated optimism, it has also prompted questions about how the government intends to finance another major spending commitment.
FREE MEALS PROGRAMME UNDER SCRUTINY
At the centre of Mr Prabowo's welfare agenda is his flagship free nutritious meals programme, aimed at combating stunting and malnutrition among children.
Despite food poisoning incidents that have raised concerns over food safety and oversight, the initiative has expanded rapidly to reach more than 57 million beneficiaries nationwide, including schoolchildren, toddlers, breastfeeding mothers and pregnant women.
At least US$15 billion has been earmarked for the initiative in next year's state budget, underscoring the significant financial resources required to sustain it and intensifying scrutiny of the government's spending priorities as it simultaneously pursues other costly programmes.
Indonesia’s parliament in September approved Mr Prabowo’s 2027 budget, with spending projected at over US$228 billion.
The growing expenditure has also revived debate over Indonesia's long-standing fiscal rules.
The country's annual budget deficit is capped at 3 per cent of gross domestic product, a restriction intended to maintain fiscal discipline and reassure investors.
Some lawmakers have called for a review of that ceiling to give the government greater flexibility to spend.
However, critics warn that relaxing the limit could weaken confidence in Indonesia's fiscal management.
“That's very risky because it implies that the government will do anything to raise funds for these priority programmes or projects,” said Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara, executive director of the Centre of Economic and Law Studies (CELIOS), a Jakarta-based public policy institution.
“The consequence is that investors and creditors may start to view Indonesia as being a little reckless.”
Last Friday (16 Oct), Indonesian stocks suffered their steepest one-day fall in nearly three decades, after index provider MSCI raised the prospect of stripping the country of its “emerging market” status.
ECONOMIC GROWTH OFFERS BRIGHT SPOT
Despite concerns over government spending, Indonesia's economy has shown resilience.
The economy expanded by 5.45 per cent in the first half of 2026, exceeding economists' expectations and prompting the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to raise its full-year growth forecast.
However, a significant portion of that expansion has been driven by public expenditure, raising questions about whether the momentum can be sustained.
Government spending rose 15.97 per cent in the second quarter, following an even sharper increase of 21.81 per cent in Q1.
Analysts say that while higher public spending can stimulate economic activity in the short term, sustained growth will also require stronger private investment, job creation and productivity gains.
That is particularly important for Mr Prabowo, who has set an ambitious target of accelerating Indonesia's economic growth to 8 per cent annually.
Last month, Mr Prabowo appointed Mr Suahasil Nazara as finance minister, placing him at the centre of efforts to balance the administration's spending ambitions with fiscal discipline.
Mr Suahasil has pledged to maintain the budget deficit below the statutory ceiling of 3 per cent of GDP, signalling continuity in the government's commitment to fiscal prudence.
However, the pressure to finance expensive welfare initiatives, infrastructure development and other national priorities could test that commitment in the years ahead.
CABINET SHAKE-UPS RAISE POLITICAL QUESTIONS
Economic challenges are not the only pressures confronting Mr Prabowo as he begins the second half of his five-year presidential term.
This month, he carried out his seventh and largest cabinet reshuffle, replacing several high-profile figures overseeing key economic, diplomatic and security portfolios.
Political observers say the shake-ups could be aimed at tightening his grip on the ruling coalition and ensuring that ministers remain aligned with his priorities, amid signs of declining public approval.
They caution that the coalition's cohesion could face growing challenges as political parties begin positioning themselves for the 2029 general election, especially if public dissatisfaction with the administration grows.
“Part of the reason why the coalition is so intact now is because everybody is compliant with Mr Prabowo … because they expect political incentives,” said Mr Djayadi Hanan, head of the political science programme at Indonesian International Islamic University.
“With the fact that the public is having more and more gap with the president, indicated at least by the very low approval rating, the political parties (looking ahead at) the next election will think (if) it’s worth it being on the side of the president.”
Further complications could emerge from efforts by some political parties to impeach Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka. Mr Gibran, the eldest son of former president Joko Widodo, has faced growing scrutiny over his educational credentials.
The Constitutional Court has dismissed a legal challenge seeking his disqualification on procedural grounds, but continued questions surrounding his vice presidency could become another source of political tension.
The issue is particularly sensitive given Mr Gibran's ties to his father, whose support played a significant role in the political alliance that brought Mr Prabowo to power in 2024.
HAZE CLOUDING FOREIGN RELATIONS
Beyond economic and political pressures, the administration is also grappling with a major environmental crisis.
Forest and land fires have been raging across parts of Indonesia for more than two months, triggering transboundary haze and raising concerns about air quality across the region.
More than 60,000 firefighters have been deployed to contain the blazes.
Indonesia has long struggled with recurring forest and peatland fires, particularly during prolonged dry periods. The resulting haze poses public health risks, disrupts economic activity and can strain diplomatic relations with neighbouring countries.
During a hybrid limited cabinet meeting last week, Mr Prabowo described the crisis as one of his administration's highest priorities and pledged to strengthen preventive measures.
“If there are any needs or requirements, tell us what you need. This is one of our highest priorities. We must address this immediately, and we must prevent it from happening again. Going forward, our campaign and strategy must be extensive, comprehensive and far-reaching, with a strong focus on prevention,” he said.
He has replaced the head of the agency responsible for firefighting and disaster relief, put in place directives against slash-and-burn practices on peatland, and prioritised fire prevention as a long-term solution.
As Mr Prabowo enters his third year in office, the challenge will be to translate his ambitious promises into tangible results while balancing public expectations with economic and political stability.
And with the 2029 election approaching, his ability to deliver could prove crucial to maintaining public confidence and the support of his political allies.

articles.title: Balancing deposit and lending interest rates. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Balancing deposit and lending interest rates.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Recently, banks have tended to increase deposit interest rates to ensure sufficient capital for lending. This will lead to a corresponding increase in lending interest rates, affecting borrowing costs and putting pressure on businesses' liquidity at the end of the year.
According to experts from SSI Securities Corporation, interest rates are the clearest indicator of the supply-demand imbalance for capital. Behind the upward trend in interest rates during the first nine months of 2026 lies the gap between credit and deposits that has accumulated since 2024, when loan growth outpaced deposit growth and rising energy prices put pressure on inflation. Banks that had aggressively increased lending in the market (where direct financial transactions take place between credit institutions and corporate and individual customers) had to increase interbank borrowing at reporting times to meet the State Bank of Vietnam's (SBV) regulations on operational safety indicators. On October 12, 2026, deposit interest rates had risen to approximately 8.3% per year at state-owned commercial banks. Interest rates range from 8.8-9.4% per year at leading joint-stock commercial banks and 9.8-10% per year at smaller joint-stock commercial banks. Meanwhile, banks are shifting towards medium- and long-term capital mobilization to bridge the shortfall and prepare for longer-term projects. Consequently, lending rates are rising, along with the first signs of slowing credit growth and pressure on asset quality.
The Vietnam Agricultural and Rural Development Bank ( Agribank ) is implementing many credit programs with preferential interest rates to support businesses in developing production and business. Photo: NGO TRANG
At a banking policy meeting held on October 19th, the Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam, Pham Duc An, emphasized: "To effectively reduce lending interest rates, credit institutions must simultaneously cut operating costs, share profits, and reduce capital mobilization costs. Deposit interest rates are one of the most important components of capital costs; if banks continue to push deposit interest rates higher, it will be difficult to find a basis for reducing lending interest rates. Interest rate reduction should not be applied indiscriminately but should be targeted, focusing on supporting priority sectors such as production and business. The policy of reducing interest rates should be considered for both existing loans and new loans. This will help operating businesses reduce their financial burden while supporting their capital needs for production and business."
You may also like
In line with the Government's policy and the State Bank of Vietnam's operational direction, Military Commercial Joint Stock Bank (MB) is implementing a comprehensive set of solutions to reduce lending interest rates, focusing on supporting priority sectors, contributing to reducing capital costs, promoting production and business, and boosting economic growth in the remaining months of 2026. Accordingly, MB is reducing lending interest rates by 1.5% per year for five priority sectors (agriculture and rural areas; export production and business; small and medium-sized enterprises; supporting industries; and high-tech enterprises), bringing the lending interest rate down to 7.9% per year. In particular, for certain priority cases, MB is considering applying interest rate reductions of up to 2% per year, creating more favorable conditions for businesses and individuals to access credit at reasonable costs. In addition, other commercial banks such as Agribank, VietinBank, BIDV , Vietcombank, etc., have also proactively reduced deposit interest rates to create a solid foundation for reducing lending interest rates and providing preferential interest rate credit packages to support businesses.
Limit the situation where banks compete to drive up deposit interest rates.
To balance deposit and lending interest rates at an appropriate level, Associate Professor Phung Thanh Quang, from the Institute of Banking and Finance, National Economics University, proposed: "First, the State Bank of Vietnam needs to flexibly use monetary policy tools, especially open market operations and refinancing, to support reasonable liquidity and limit the situation where banks compete to push deposit interest rates higher.
However, liquidity provision must be linked to the goals of controlling inflation, stabilizing exchange rates, and ensuring the safety of the system.
Second, it is necessary to strengthen supervision of capital utilization, especially the risk of maturity mismatch and concentrated credit in sectors with long capital recovery cycles.
At the same time, promote the handling of bad debts, improve credit quality and capital turnover efficiency, thereby reducing liquidity pressure from within the banking system.
Third, the State Bank of Vietnam needs to encourage commercial banks to reduce operating costs, improve management efficiency, and share some of the pressure of increasing capital costs.
" This applies to businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises, manufacturing and export businesses, and priority sectors.
An increase in deposit interest rates does not necessarily mean a corresponding increase in lending interest rates.
In the long term, it is necessary to develop the capital market, especially the corporate bond market and medium- and long-term capital raising channels, in order to reduce the economy's excessive dependence on bank credit.
"
You may also like
Customers conducting transactions at Military Commercial Joint Stock Bank (MB). Photo: PHUONG ANH
Maintaining stable lending interest rates at appropriate levels to reduce the burden of borrowing costs, support business recovery, and boost production and business activities is a crucial task for the banking sector. Successful implementation requires close attention and guidance from the State Bank of Vietnam, as well as profit sharing, preferential interest rate support, and simplified and expedited lending procedures from commercial banks for businesses and households nationwide. This will contribute to achieving the double-digit growth targets set for this year and the following years.

articles.title: Corporate bonds face double pressure: rising interest rates and a surge in maturities. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Corporate bonds face double pressure: rising interest rates and a surge in maturities.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
The corporate bond market is expected to slow down in Q3 2026 as interest rates rise, while maturities are projected to reach VND 276 trillion in 2027.
According to S&I Ratings' Q3 2026 bond market report, companies successfully issued 153 bond tranches during the quarter, with a total value of VND 179,400 billion, a decrease of 26% compared to Q2 2026 but an increase of 7.8% compared to the same period last year.
This development indicates that the market has adjusted after the strong surge in Q2/2026. Nevertheless, public offerings (POs) recorded remarkable results, reaching VND 31,600 billion across 16 tranches, a 55% increase year-on-year and the highest level ever. Of these, commercial banks conducted 8 tranches, with Agribank alone raising VND 15,000 billion.
For the first nine months of the year, the value of maturing bonds reached VND 132,800 billion, a 5.7% increase compared to the same period last year, while the amount repurchased before maturity reached VND 228,600 billion, a 4.5% decrease. The net issuance value reached VND 102,600 billion, bringing the outstanding corporate bond debt to approximately VND 1.54 million billion at the end of September, a 7.1% increase compared to the end of 2025.
However, the bond market's growth rate remains lower than the 9% GDP growth and 11.59% credit growth in the first nine months of the year. According to S&I Ratings, high credit demand is putting pressure on interest rates, increasing the cost of capital for businesses.
Real estate issuance has slowed, and the banking sector has not yet shown a clear recovery.
In the third quarter of 2026, real estate bond issuance activity decreased significantly after a sharp increase in the previous quarter. The number of issuances fell from 43 to 21, while the total value decreased by 55% compared to the second quarter of 2026.
Vingroup alone issued VND 16,000 billion in Q3 2026, lower than the VND 61,000 billion of the previous quarter. Meanwhile, Masterise maintained an issuance value of approximately VND 23,500 billion. These two groups of businesses account for a large proportion of the real estate sector's bond issuance activities.
Despite a quarterly decline, real estate bond issuance still increased by 27% year-on-year. Overall, in the first nine months, the value of issuances in this sector increased by 121% compared to the same period in 2025.
You may also like
According to S&I Ratings, the strong capital needs of real estate companies remain a key driver for the bond market.
However, high interest rates can increase the cost of capital, affecting project implementation progress and the ability of businesses to raise resources.
In the banking sector, the value of issuances in Q3 2026 reached approximately VND 120,000 billion, an increase of 7% compared to the previous quarter and 11.8% compared to the same period last year. Despite the improvement in the quarter, the total value of issuances by this group in the first nine months was still about 20% lower than the same period last year.
The report suggests that the regulations in Circular 50 regarding the calculation of the loan-to-deposit ratio (LDR), which stipulate that only bonds meeting Tier 2 capital requirements are included in the denominator, have affected the issuance incentives of banks.
Since banks accounted for approximately 52% of the total value of corporate bond issuances in 2026, a slowdown in this sector also contributed to the overall market's slower growth.
Bond yields are rising, increasing pressure to mature in 2027.
The pressure of capital costs continues to be reflected in issuance interest rates. According to S&I Ratings, corporate bond yields have increased by an average of about 2.5 percentage points from their 2025 lows, although the rate of increase showed signs of slowing down in the third quarter of 2026.
For the banking sector, the average issuance interest rate reached 8.85% per year, higher than the average of 8.7% per year in 2022. Most issuances had interest rates ranging from 8-9.7% per year, while some exceeded 10% per year.
In the real estate sector, issuance interest rates could reach 12.5-13% per year, although still lower than the previously recorded peak of 14-14.5% per year. The average interest rate for this sector in the third quarter of 2026 is approximately 11.5% per year.
This development indicates that businesses are facing higher funding costs amidst continued increases in medium- and long-term capital demand. This pressure is particularly noticeable for businesses with high financial leverage or those requiring significant funding for project implementation.
You may also like
According to estimates by S&I Ratings, approximately VND 93 trillion in corporate bonds will mature in the fourth quarter of 2026, the highest level for the year. Of this amount, real estate bonds account for about VND 46.9 trillion, nearly half of the total value.
In 2027, the value of maturing bonds is expected to reach approximately VND 276 trillion, a 22% increase compared to 2026. The real estate sector alone accounts for about VND 156 trillion, equivalent to 57% of the total maturing value.
In this context, new bond issuances not only serve investment and project development needs but also help businesses restructure maturing debts. This is considered one of the factors maintaining the demand for capital mobilization through bonds in the coming period.
However, the market outlook remains pressured by the cost of capital. S&I Ratings believes that inflation risks and high international government bond yields could keep domestic interest rates under pressure, at least in the first half of 2027.
In the medium term, capital demand for real estate, transportation infrastructure, energy, and industry, along with refinancing pressure, is expected to support the corporate bond market. However, according to this unit's assessment, the market still needs more time for sustainable restructuring and expansion of its investor base.

articles.title: Interest rates remain high, homebuyers are cautious. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Interest rates remain high, homebuyers are cautious.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
High lending interest rates have made homebuyers more cautious, impacting the absorption capacity and liquidity of the real estate market. Experts expect that interest rates will gradually cool down in the near future, making homebuyers more accessible.
In a newly released report, MBS Securities stated that the average 12-month deposit interest rate has increased by approximately 0.3 percentage points compared to the previous quarter, pushing lending rates at most banks above 10%. This continues to lead investors to maintain a more cautious stance towards real estate.
According to the Dat Xanh Services Institute for Economic , Financial, and Real Estate Research (DXS-FERI), high interest rates and limited credit limits have significantly impacted purchasing decisions, leading to increased caution and delay.

Tìm hiểu lịch sử
Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch
Khám phá ĐNA
For buyers, the pressure of debt repayment after the preferential period makes the use of leverage, especially long-term loans, more carefully considered. Liquidity in some segments therefore slows down. For developers, increased financing costs also narrow profit margins and affect project implementation progress.
In the third quarter of 2026, the fixed interest rate for the first 12 months of real estate loans was commonly between 8.5% and 11.5% per annum. After the preferential period ended, the floating interest rate rose to 13%-15% per annum. Compared to the first two quarters of the year, the floating rate has increased by one notch, with rates fluctuating between 12% and 14% in the first and second quarters of 2026.
Interest rates have directly impacted real estate liquidity. According to a report by the Ministry of Construction , in the third quarter of 2026, access to credit for businesses and homebuyers remained difficult, and rising capital costs affected purchasing power, absorption capacity, and market liquidity.
According to reports from 27 out of 34 localities, the inventory of real estate in projects in the third quarter of 2026 was approximately 51,950 units/plots, higher than the previous quarter. Nationwide, there are still about 5,012 projects facing difficulties and obstacles that need to be addressed.
The market is dependent on interest rate movements.
Purchasing power is expected to depend significantly on interest rate movements in the final months of the year. DXS-FERI estimates that with home loan interest rates around 10-12% per year, the housing market absorption rate may only reach about 40%; if interest rates float to 13-15%, the absorption rate could fall below 20%.
You may also like
Mr. Luu Van Anh (currently residing in building S1, Goldmark City apartment complex, Ho Tung Mau Street, Phu Dien Ward, Hanoi ) said that recently, due to rising interest rates, he has temporarily stopped buying for investment purposes and is only maintaining his work connecting and distributing secondary apartments between homeowners and those in need.
According to him, in recent months, the prices of many secondary apartments have started to fall, with some owners needing money urgently and facing financial pressure, thus lowering prices quite significantly. However, when considering buying for investment purposes, he continues to hesitate due to the relatively high interest rates.
According to Ms. Nguyen Hoai An, Senior Director of CBRE Hanoi Branch, from the beginning of 2026 until now, the Hanoi housing market has undergone a rebalancing cycle after about two years of continuous growth.
Although supply is expected to be more abundant in 2026, liquidity will be highly differentiated. Only products with complete legal documentation, advantageous locations, meeting real needs, or with competitive sales policies will be able to maintain good sales volumes.
Notably, interest rate pressure has been acting as a "natural filter," accelerating the differentiation between developers with strong financial capabilities and those with limited financial flexibility.
According to Ms. An, for the final quarter of 2026, interest rate movements and the decisions of major developers to release new properties will be the two main variables determining market dynamics.
Expectations for lower interest rates
Ms. Nguyen Hong Van, Senior Director and Head of Hanoi Market at JLL Vietnam, stated that the demand for loans to develop projects from investors is very high, while access to these loans is not easy.
"The impact of interest rates affects both developers and homebuyers. For buyers, the impact of interest rates is most evident in the residential real estate segment," Ms. Van said.
According to Mr. Le Dinh Chung, General Director of SGO Homes Real Estate Consulting and Development Joint Stock Company, and Vice Chairman of the Market Research and Evaluation Council of the Vietnam Association of Real Estate Brokers (VARS), besides land and legal aspects, capital is one of the key factors for real estate businesses. Every percentage increase in interest expense significantly impacts total costs, especially sales costs.
You may also like
For projects with a total investment of 1,000-2,000 billion VND, the current cost of capital averages 12-14% per year, creating significant pressure compared to the previous 8-10%.
Mr. Chung predicted that in the near future, lending interest rates are likely to only be adjusted slightly. This means that difficulties in accessing capital for businesses may still persist. However, with current policy directives, Mr. Chung expects borrowing costs to gradually decrease.
At a recent real estate seminar held in Hanoi, economist Associate Professor Ngo Tri Long stated that for homebuyers, rising interest rates mean a larger loan repayment amount. This forces many to reduce their home buying budget, extend their savings period, or postpone their purchase decisions.
Meanwhile, real estate businesses that use high financial leverage may face more serious consequences in terms of cash flow and debt repayment ability. High interest rates do not necessarily cause an immediate decrease in asking prices, but they can weaken liquidity and increase pressure to adjust actual transaction prices.
If this situation persists, businesses that rely heavily on borrowed capital and have low product sales potential will face significant financial pressure, and may even be forced to adjust their business strategies and pricing.

Ho Chi Minh City (VNS/VNA) - Vietnam’s growing role in global manufacturing, record foreign investment disbursement and fast-expanding digital economy are further strengthening the country's position as one of Asia Pacific’s most compelling growth markets. 
This momentum will take centre stage when the 2027 World Trade Centres Association (WTCA) Global Business Forum (GBF) convenes at Binh Duong Ward, Ho Chi Minh City, from April 4 to 7, 2027. 
Hosted by WTCA in partnership with World Trade Centre Binh Duong New City (WTC BDNC), the forum will bring international business leaders and investors together in one of the country’s most important industrial centres to explore new opportunities in trade, investment, manufacturing, technology and supply chain development. 
Vietnam enters its next phase of growth from a position of economic strength. Its total registered foreign investment (FDI) reached 38.4 billion USD in 2025, while disbursed FDI rose 9% to a record 27.6 billion USD. These figures point to sustained investor confidence despite a more complex global trade environment. 
The country’s appeal extends beyond cost competitiveness. Its strategic location in Southeast Asia, extensive network of trade agreements, including the EU–Vietnam Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA) and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), and established export base give companies access to regional and global markets. As businesses pursue China+1 strategies, Vietnam offers a credible platform for diversifying production while remaining connected to Asian supply chains. 
“As global businesses navigate evolving trade policies and market dynamics, the ability to build trusted international connections has become more important than ever,” said Scott Wang, WTCA Vice President, Asia Pacific. 
“Vietnam’s rise as a manufacturing, technology and innovation hub reflects the broader opportunities emerging across Asia Pacific. 
"Through WTCA’s extensive global network, we are committed to connecting businesses with the partners, market intelligence and opportunities they need to grow with confidence.” 
The GBF builds on discussions at the 56th Annual WTCA GBF in Philadelphia, US, hosted by WTC Greater Philadelphia in April 2026, where more than 500 leaders from over 50 countries and territories examined how trusted relationships, regional partnerships and cross-border collaboration can help businesses respond to geopolitical uncertainty and supply chain disruption. 
Bringing the next forum to Vietnam is expected to shift that global conversation towards practical investment and partnership opportunities in one of the region’s fastest-growing economies. 
By hosting the 2027 WTCA GBF, Vietnam will strengthen its position as a preferred destination for diversified manufacturing, and will allow it to develop further the technology, skills and industrial ecosystems required for its next stage of growth. 
For Vietnamese businesses, the GBF will provide direct access to WTCA’s network of more than 300 highly connected businesses and organisations in nearly 100 countries and territories, opening new channels for investment, market entry and international collaboration. /.

articles.title: Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien attends the review meeting for two draft laws. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien attends the review meeting for two draft laws.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
On the afternoon of October 20th, at the National Assembly building, Central Committee member and Vice Chairman of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien attended the plenary session of the Economic and Financial Committee to review the draft Law on Land (amended) and the draft Law on Real Estate Business (amended).
Member of the Central Committee of the Party, Chairman of the Economic and Financial Committee Phan Van Mai presided over the meeting.
Attending the session were representatives from the Standing Committee of the National Assembly, the Committees of the National Assembly; representatives from the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Construction; representatives from the Central Party Office, the Government Office, ministries and agencies, the State Audit Office, the Vietnam Federation of Trade and Industry, and representatives from the People's Committees of Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi, Da Nang, Hai Phong, Can Tho, Quang Ninh, Bac Ninh and Hue.
Regulate the added value from land appropriately for the development of rental housing.
Reporting on the ongoing improvements to the draft Law on Land (amended), Deputy Minister of Agriculture and Environment Dang Ngoc Diep stated that the draft Law has incorporated and refined many regulations regarding the scope of application; land allocation, land leasing, and land use conversion; the authority of state management of land; and the land fund for payment under BT contracts.
Regarding the rights and obligations of land users, the draft Law continues to refine regulations on land subdivision and consolidation; notarization and authentication of contracts exercising land use rights; and conditions for exercising rights for land leased with annual payments, ensuring that no rights stipulated in the 2024 Land Law are omitted.
Regarding land acquisition, the draft Law refines regulations on land acquisition for projects in surrounding areas and infrastructure works; requiring that the list of projects and works subject to land acquisition be approved by the Provincial People's Council. At the same time, it refines regulations on land acquisition due to non-use or delayed use; removing the case where the State acquires land to create a land fund to pay for projects under BT contracts and land acquisition for logistics center projects serving seaports, airports, and inland waterways with a land use scale exceeding 50 hectares.
The draft law also supplements and refines regulations on the reimbursement of compensation, support, and resettlement funds advanced for investment projects that have ceased operation; and the exchange of confiscated residential land for land of another plot owned by the land user within the same commune.
The delegates acknowledged the efforts of the drafting agency in incorporating and revising the draft, and requested further review to ensure the timely and full institutionalization of the Party's policies and guidelines.
Delegates emphasized the need to ensure consistency and uniformity between the Land Law, the Real Estate Business Law, the Housing Law, and related laws such as the Investment Law, the Construction Law, the Law on Expropriation and Requisition of Assets, and the Oil and Gas Law. Transitional provisions also need to be reviewed and improved to avoid legal gaps.
Regarding the draft Law on Land (amended), some opinions have focused on the management and use of land by privatized enterprises. These opinions suggest that the regulations in the draft law do not fully address the difficulties and confusion faced by localities. Therefore, it is necessary to study and add provisions allowing enterprises to continue using land in accordance with the purpose of asset use and the capital allocated to those assets that were formed when they were state-owned enterprises.
You may also like
Some opinions suggest that appropriate policies need to be reviewed and studied to address the situation where garden and pond land within the same plot as a house is often mistakenly treated as agricultural land for rice or other crops when the State reclaims the land. This significant discrepancy is the main reason why people do not agree when the State reclaims land.
In addition, delegates proposed a more detailed clarification of the requirements in Resolution No. 21-NQ/TW, especially the policy on reasonably regulating the added value from land for the development of rental housing and the implementation of social welfare policies, ensuring consistency with the draft amended Housing Law. State capital from the housing fund is expected to provide a significant resource for the development of rental housing in the future.
No adverse retroactive application and absolutely no legalization of wrongdoing.
Speaking at the session, Vice Chairman of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien acknowledged the efforts of the drafting agency, the reviewing agency, and related agencies in researching and coordinating the revision of the two draft laws. However, some contents have not been fully incorporated, especially the requirements of Resolution No. 18-NQ/TW and Resolution No. 29-NQ/TW of the Central Committee.
The Vice Chairman of the National Assembly requested continued review and refinement of the draft laws, ensuring the full institutionalization of the Party's guidelines and policies, especially those directed by the Central Committee, the Politburo, the Secretariat, and competent authorities regarding land and real estate business.
According to the Vice Chairman of the National Assembly, many practical obstacles have been clearly identified; the important issue now is how to institutionalize solutions to fundamentally address the shortcomings caused by legal regulations. Therefore, the draft Law must thoroughly resolve the practical obstacles that have been observed and pointed out.
The Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly also noted that it is not possible to simply include the spirit and principles in the law in a general way and then leave the important contents to decrees and guiding circulars. The core principles, policies, and issues within the authority of the National Assembly that directly affect the rights and interests of citizens and businesses must be clearly stipulated in the law.
Along with a strong shift towards modern land management thinking and the development of a healthy and sustainable real estate market, it is necessary to strictly enforce the requirements for controlling power and preventing and combating corruption and negative practices in lawmaking.
In particular, the Vice Chairman of the National Assembly requested a thorough identification of regulations that risk creating loopholes for favoritism, collusion in land auctions, policy abuse, the formation of interest groups, or causing losses to the state budget. Resolving difficulties must go hand in hand with preventing the exploitation of policies for personal gain and the loss of resources.
You may also like
Regarding the consistency of the legal system, the Vice Chairman of the National Assembly suggested a thorough review of the relationship between the Land Law, the Real Estate Business Law, and the Housing Law, to avoid overlaps and conflicts during implementation.
“If regulations are found to have the potential to create a system of favoritism or are inadequate beyond the authority of the reviewing agency, the reviewing agency and related agencies must frankly report and propose solutions; they must not conceal anything. From Market Opinions to On-Chain Signals
Prediction markets are increasingly becoming an interface for turning expectations about future events into market signals. For Probly, TOKEN2049 provided an opportunity to bring that idea directly to an audience already accustomed to trading changing market conditions, information, and expectations.
The name Probly comes from “probably,” the word people use when the outcome of an event remains uncertain. It is also inspired by P(A), the mathematical notation used to represent the probability of an event.
Probly currently supports 5,100 events and 47,000 markets across Sports, Geopolitics, Crypto, Finance, Economy, and Politics. The platform also offers 172 active live markets for same-day trading, including high-frequency Crypto “Up or Down” rolling markets across BTC, ETH, SOL, and XRP.

For Probly, these conversations reinforced an important direction for the product: prediction markets should not be limited to occasional major events. They can become a more active interface for following changing information, forming a view, and trading expectations as events develop.
What Comes Next for Probly
Following TOKEN2049 Singapore, Probly will continue developing its prediction market experience around accessibility, broader event coverage, frequent trading opportunities, and transparent on-chain infrastructure.
The company will also continue working with ecosystem and infrastructure partners as it develops new ways for users to express views on future outcomes through on-chain markets.
TOKEN2049 and WHALE3RA marked another step in bringing Probly’s core idea to a wider audience: uncertainty is everywhere, and markets can make collective expectations around what happens next more visible, transparent, and useful.

Blockchain Deposit Insurance Corporation (“BDIC”), a decentralized cryptocurrency deposit insurer providing coverage for digital assets, today announced the establishment of its Singapore business operations and announced that the BDIC Coin Token Sale is targeted for the first quarter of 2027, and that it has engaged Cole-Frieman & Mallon LLP as outside counsel in the United States.
PRESS RELEASE SUMMARY
BDIC’s Singapore entity (BDIC SG PTE LTD located on Lorong Ampas in Singapore) is intended to serve as the primary insurance underwriting hub for the company. The company will engage local legal representation and begin the regulatory engagement process for the new insurance entity for approval under the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and in the meantime, the company plans to place coverage for clients’ needs through existing dedicated insurance cells issued through network partners while awaiting its appointment and approval to write policy coverage directly. During this period, a Cayman Islands BDIC Foundation and its British Virgin Islands subsidiary will be established to issue the BDIC Coin independently of BDIC. BDIC Coin is intended to be used to pay BDIC insurance premiums, settlements, and governance as a true utility payment token.

Why BDIC Singapore?
BDIC selected Singapore as the second location after BDIC HK as it is the intended primary insurance underwriting hub because of the depth of the jurisdiction’s financial regulation and its position in Asian digital asset markets. Asia has moved ahead of much of the world in digital asset adoption and market awareness, and BDIC’s operational strategy is designed to meet the requirements set out by MAS rather than work around them, as Singapore’s leadership and advanced vision on crypto insurance is the perfect platform.
“Establishing our presence in Singapore is more than a geographic expansion from our location in Hong Kong. As we have engaged local representation and will submit the required information in the coming weeks, we look forward to working with the MAS team for our approval”.
Regulatory and Compliance Architecture
According to BDIC’s compliance team, BDIC is considering partnering with an existing local insurance partner, but it is not required in order to operate under the Insurance Act, administered by MAS. BDIC’s operations are also designed to align with Singapore’s broader digital asset statutes, including the Payment Services Act 2019 (PSA) and the Financial Services and Markets Act 2022 (FSMA), which govern digital payment token services, including custody.
Cross-border insurance carries jurisdiction-specific obligations, and BDIC is structuring its global offering to satisfy local mandates in the jurisdictions where its policyholders reside, but also for global reach. While the Singapore hub is intended to serve as the primary underwriting engine, BDIC intends to serve policyholders in other jurisdictions through structured reinsurance partnerships, risk ceding, or partnerships with admitted local carriers in Europe, for instance. BDIC is also implementing asset valuation protocols that include independent custody verification and cold-to-hot wallet storage ratios consistent with international auditing standards, where applicable.

These controls will create the next version of traditional finance, a stable environment in which consumers and businesses alike can operate globally. MAS guidelines are an example of what BDIC wanted as a framework from the start.”
Legal and Infrastructure
BDIC’s CEO centered comments around commitment to building its platform on a properly established legal and compliance foundation. Subsequently, the company has engaged Cole-Frieman & Mallon LLP as outside counsel in the United States moving forward accordingly.

Judicial Commissioner Isa Aziz Ibrahim said Akmal’s remarks went beyond legitimate political debate and carried a serious defamatory implication against Kok.
“The said video did carry a severe defamatory sting that the plaintiff habitually and continually destabilises national harmony,” he said in his grounds of judgment dated Oct 19 when ruling on Kok’s defamation suit against Akmal.
The case stems from a video Akmal posted on TikTok, Facebook and Instagram in September 2024 after Kok questioned a proposal to make halal certification compulsory for restaurants and food businesses that did not serve pork or alcohol.
Kok had warned that the proposal could burden businesses, particularly smaller operators. Akmal responded by calling her an “old nyonya,” telling her to keep quiet, and suggesting that a “non-halal” label be placed on her forehead.
The judge rejected Akmal’s defence of fair comment, saying there was no factual basis for his allegation that Kok habitually disrupted national harmony.
“A defendant cannot invent or extrapolate unproven facts and comment upon them,” he said.
Isa also rejected Akmal’s claim of qualified privilege, citing the wide dissemination of the remarks and the personal attacks against Kok.
He noted that Akmal admitted recording the video in anger without seeking clarification, and that his primary motive was to attack Kok personally.
Akmal also kept the video online and neither apologised nor retracted his remarks.
The court also dismissed the argument that Kok had provoked the dispute through her Facebook post.
“An imperfect translation or unfortunate word choice by an elected official is not a licence for an opponent to execute an unevidenced character assassination,” Isa said.
The judge awarded Kok RM250,000 in general and aggravated damages.
He also ordered Akmal to remove the video from his social media accounts within seven days, barred him from republishing the defamatory remarks or words to the same effect, and ordered him to pay RM50,000 in costs.

Earlier, on the evening of June 23 and early morning of June 24, the Immigration Management Division under Dong Nai City Police, in coordination with relevant units, conducted simultaneous administrative inspections at 12 accommodation establishments in Tran Bien and Tam Hiep wards.

Initial investigations found that a total of 43 foreigners had illegally entered Vietnam and failed to declare their temporary residence as required by law.
Renting houses to illegally accommodate foreigners
Further investigation found that Nguyen Thi Thuy Linh, 30, a resident in Tran Bien Ward, played a key role in arranging accommodation for the foreigners.
Linh had been living as husband and wife with Li Kun, a Chinese national, since 2017, and they have a child together.
In early May 2026, Li Kun was hired through a WhatsApp account named “Co Co” to find accommodation for around 30 foreigners coming to Vietnam to livestream sales.
Li Kun and Linh initially rented a house on Vo Thi Sau Street to accommodate the group. The foreigners were later moved elsewhere by “Co Co.”
Linh later rented two houses, A34 and A35, on D5 Street, and apartment B1801 in the Topaz Twins apartment building to accommodate the foreigners.
Investigators found that Linh personally signed the rental contracts and received rent payments from Li Kun and the foreigners.
She also hired workers to carry out repairs, install cameras, and purchase beds, mattresses and household items for the foreigners' accommodation.
Several foreigners staying illegally in Dong Nai were discovered. Photo: Provided by police
Go Qing, a Chinese national, had asked Linh to help arrange the rental of house A26B on Pham Van Nghia Street in April 2026 to accommodate several foreigners staying in Vietnam illegally, investigators found.
During questioning, Go Qing was unable to produce valid documents for the foreigners.
Police determined that Linh had rented apartment B1801 under her name for Zhao Hong, a Chinese national, to accommodate three foreigners.
Two had entered Vietnam legally but their temporary residence had not been declared, while the third lacked valid entry documents.
Zhao Hong left Vietnam on June 23, but the three foreigners continued to stay in the country illegally.
A group of foreigners who entered and stayed in Vietnam illegally. Photo provided by police
Property fraud and gambling cases uncovered
During the investigation, police also found that Linh had recruited Lang Hoai Lam, 27, from Lang Son Province, Tran Van Dung, 32, from Ha Tinh Province, and Li Yan, 39, a Chinese national and Li Kun's older brother, to use computer networks, telecommunications networks and electronic devices to commit property fraud.

Police seized five computers, 11 mobile phones and a tablet.
On July 2, the Investigation Police Agency under Dong Nai City Police initiated legal proceedings against Linh for illegally using computer networks, telecommunications networks and electronic devices to appropriate property.
Linh, who was raising a young child, was banned from leaving her place of residence.

On July 3, police initiated a criminal case and prosecuted three Chinese nationals, Han Xu, 32, Lin Kang Ling, 22, and Song Yue Qi, 37, for gambling.
On July 6, police initiated a criminal case and prosecuted Li Kun, placing him in temporary detention.
The Investigation Police Agency under Dong Nai City Police has issued investigation conclusions in the cases and forwarded them to the same-level People's Procuracy, recommending the prosecution of the defendants in accordance with the law.

Petronas wants to expand cooperation with Vietnam on long-term LNG supply contracts and has proposed working with state-run Petrovietnam and Vietnamese companies to develop LNG infrastructure and new energy value chains, including wind power, hydrogen and carbon capture and storage (CCS), as well as facilitate technology transfer.
The Malaysian national oil and gas corporation's group president and CEO Tengku Muhammad Taufik made the remarks during a meeting with Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung in Hanoi last Friday, on the sidelines of a visit to Vietnam by a Petronas delegation.
Taufik thanked the Vietnamese leader for supporting Petronas’s cooperation and projects in Vietnam. He also conveyed greetings from Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim to Hung.
Reporting on effective cooperation with Vietnamese ministries, agencies and Petrovietnam in recent years, which he said offered considerable prospects, Taufik said Petronas wanted to deepen ties and work with Petrovietnam and Vietnamese partners to advance their shared vision, particularly under their Strategic Alliance Agreement (SAA).
The cooperation aims to help ensure energy security at affordable costs and support economic growth in both countries, in line with directives from the two prime ministers and the governments’ shared priorities in the sector. The parties also seek to advance the Vietnam-Malaysia-Singapore (VMS) power grid interconnection project.
Welcoming the Petronas chief to Vietnam, Hung acknowledged the group’s efforts and contributions to oil and gas exploration, development and production in both Vietnam and Malaysia.
The prime minister praised Petronas and Petrovietnam for building a strong, long-standing partnership over more than 30 years through joint efforts to support Vietnam’s energy security, sustainable development and economic growth, as well as those of the wider Asian region.
He described the two groups as trusted partners and an example of effective, long-term strategic cooperation that benefits both sides.
The cabinet leader also stressed the importance of maintaining stable operations at the PM3-CAA oil and gas project in the overlapping area between Vietnam and Malaysia.
The project has produced a cumulative 250 million barrels of oil and 43 billion cubic meters of gas, generating total revenue of more than $25 billion. It plays a key role in ensuring energy and food security and supporting economic development in Vietnam’s southwestern region.
Noting that closer cooperation between the two groups had also been an important topic in his discussions with the Malaysian prime minister, Hung said the Vietnamese government supported Petronas’s continued studies and expansion of investment, as well as the signing of new petroleum contracts for open blocks on Vietnam’s continental shelf.
Such activities must ensure investment efficiency and balance the interests of all stakeholders, including the state, businesses and investors, while complying with Vietnamese law and international law, he said.
Hung noted Vietnam was continuing to amend and improve regulations governing oil and gas, electricity, investment and land, among other areas. The country was also revising the Power Development Plan VIII (PDP VIII) and significantly streamlining administrative procedures to facilitate electricity and energy projects and meet the substantial power demand generated by economic growth.
The prime minister praised Petronas’s coordinating role and the active participation of PTSC, a subsidiary of Petrovietnam, in the Vietnam-Malaysia-Singapore (VMS) power grid interconnection project.
The Vietnamese government supports the project as a symbol of regional energy connectivity and a contribution to realizing the ASEAN Power Grid vision, he said.
Hung congratulated Petronas and Petrovietnam on recently signing the SAA, which elevates their relationship from cooperation on individual projects to a strategic alliance spanning the entire energy value chain. The agreement also helps give practical effect to the Vietnam-Malaysia Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.
He urged the two groups to put their joint coordination mechanism into operation soon and translate the agreement into substantive, effective projects and cooperation programs.
The Vietnamese government would continue to facilitate projects that comply with national plans and Vietnamese law, Hung said, adding that ministries and agencies would be instructed to support businesses and investors and help resolve difficulties arising during project implementation.
Hung expressed his hope that cooperation between Petronas and Petrovietnam would continue to grow and become a successful example of the Vietnam-Malaysia Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. He also conveyed his greetings to the Malaysian prime minister.
