(Dan Tri Newspaper) - When long-term deposit interest rates peak, the gap between economic growth and stock market performance will narrow. The P/E valuation of the VN-Index is at its lowest level since the tariff period.
In the morning trading session of October 20th, the stock market continued to disappoint as the VN-Index fell further to 1,680 points, losing nearly 9 points compared to the previous session. The continuous decline of the market over the past month has caused the general index to successively break through the support levels of 1,800 points and 1,700 points.
Liquidity hit a record low, with trading value on the HoSE exchange reaching just over 3,600 billion VND by 10:30 AM. Foreign investors continued to be net sellers. Many investors are discouraged and reluctant to trade stocks due to losses in their portfolios.
Even with positive news about the business results of many companies during the third-quarter earnings reporting season, the stock market remains subdued.
In Dragon Capital's recently released September market update report, the fund's experts analyzed that Vietnam's economy grew by nearly 10% in the third quarter, while the stock market underwent a correction. These two developments are related, as investment activity both fuels economic growth and increases capital demand, putting pressure on funding costs. In September, the stock market primarily reflected the impact of rising capital costs.
FTSE Russell's upgrade of the Vietnamese stock market on September 21st was not enough to reverse the net selling trend by foreign investors, who continued to net sell another $187 million on the HoSE exchange. The average daily trading value reached $508 million (approximately VND 13,200 billion/session) - the lowest level since the beginning of the year. The securities and real estate sectors experienced the sharpest declines under pressure from interest rates, while the energy sector led the gains thanks to rising oil prices.
Nevertheless, experts at Dragon Capital expect the gap between economic growth and stock market performance to gradually narrow as long-term deposit interest rates peak. Some initial signals indicate that the balance between capital mobilization and credit is improving. VND-denominated capital mobilization growth reached 11.7% year-to-date, exceeding credit growth of 10.1%.

"These developments reflect a decrease in demand for VND loans as interest rates rise, while depositors are responding to more attractive deposit interest rates. Banks are also increasing USD lending; mobilizing or planning to mobilize approximately $6.2 billion through loans and bond issuances in the international market," analyzed an expert from this investment fund.
However, according to experts, interest rates can only be significantly reduced when more substantial capital is injected into the system, through the State Bank's spot USD purchase, targeted refinancing measures, or accelerated disbursement of budget funds. The fiscal channel is showing positive developments, with public investment disbursement reaching 62.9% of the annual plan, 12.9 percentage points higher than the same period last year.
At the same time, the VND has appreciated by 0.8% against the USD since the beginning of the year, creating more room for the State Bank of Vietnam to buy foreign currency. However, inflation remains a limiting factor in the ability to ease policy, with the average CPI for the first nine months at 4.5%, touching the lower end of the 4.5-5% target, indicating that targeted support measures would be more appropriate than broad-based policy easing.
Regarding the stock market, Dragon Capital believes that current market valuations have largely reflected the pressure from interest rates. The VN-Index is trading at a P/E valuation of 13.5 times based on the last 12 months' earnings. However, the five leading stocks that have driven the index since the beginning of the year, including VIC, VHM, VPL, STB, and LPB, have resulted in both higher valuations and performance of the overall index compared to the rest of the market.
If these five stocks are excluded, the VN-Index has fallen by as much as 9.4% since the beginning of the year and is trading at a P/E ratio of 11.4 times, lower than the low point during the period of volatility due to tariffs in April 2025 and approaching the lows of 2020 and 2022.
With economic growth nearing 10% and the balance between capital mobilization and lending beginning to improve, the correlation between expected returns and risk at the current level is relatively attractive. The process of improving valuations will require more time until deposit interest rates begin to cool down.

Bond issuance slows down in a high-interest-rate environment.
 According to the Q3 2026 Corporate Bond Market Report by S&I Ratings ( SSI Securities Joint Stock Company), corporate bond issuance activity slowed down in Q3 2026. During the quarter, the market recorded 153 successful corporate bond issuances with a total issuance value of VND 179,400 billion, a sharp decrease of 26% compared to Q2.
 High interest rates are one of the reasons for this situation. Interest rates on bond issuances in Q3 2026 tended to increase across all sectors. Specifically, coupon rates for the banking sector were commonly in the range of 8% - 9.7% per year, with some issuances exceeding 10% per year, such as Sacombank and PVcomBank (10.5% per year). Thus, bank bond interest rates have surpassed their peak from 2022-2023.
 Interest rates for the real estate sector and other businesses have also increased sharply to 12.5% - 13% per year, but are still below the previous peak (14%-14.5% per year).
 A bright spot in the market was the record-high level of publicly issued bonds, despite the overall market slowdown. Specifically, the public issuance channel recorded impressive results with 16 successful issuances in the quarter, totaling VND 31,600 billion, a 55% increase compared to the same period last year and the highest level ever recorded.
 Commercial banks remain the most advantageous issuers and account for the largest share of publicly issued bonds, representing half of the issuances (8 out of 16), with issuance values mainly ranging from VND 1,000 to VND 3,000 billion, and Agribank alone successfully issuing VND 15 trillion.
 In addition, non-bank issuers also participated more in the public channel, with 8 issuances by securities companies (ACBS, TCBS), finance companies (F88), and consumer goods companies ( Masan MeatLife, Thuan Duc); however, the issuance scale was quite small, mostly under 1,000 billion VND.
 In the first nine months of the year, a total of 464.1 trillion VND worth of bonds were issued. After deducting the value of maturing and early redemption bonds, the net value of issued bonds was 102.6 trillion VND. Thus, the total value of outstanding bonds increased only slightly by 7.1% compared to the end of 2025, reaching 1.54 trillion VND.
 Compared to the GDP growth rate of 9% in the first nine months of 2026 and credit growth of 11.59%, the corporate bond market is expected to grow relatively slowly in 2026. High credit demand has pushed interest rates up sharply, significantly impacting the cost of capital for businesses.
 In addition, businesses also need to prepare for strict compliance requirements after Decree 200/2026/ND-CP is issued and takes effect from June 5, 2026.
 Real estate bond issuance decreased by 55% compared to the previous quarter.
 According to S&I Ratings, in the third quarter, real estate bond issuance adjusted from its peak levels. In Q3/2026, the real estate sector failed to maintain the high issuance rate of the second quarter, with the number of successful issuances decreasing from 43 to 21, and the value of issuances decreasing by 55% compared to the second quarter.
 In particular, the issuance value of the Vingroup group decreased sharply from VND 61,000 billion in Q2/2026 to VND 16,000 billion in Q3/2026, while the issuance of the Masterise group remained stable at VND 23,500 billion in Q3. These two groups of businesses typically account for up to 80% of the total issuance volume of the real estate sector and have the main impact on the group's issuance results.
 Despite a sharp decline compared to the previous quarter, the issuance volume of the Real Estate sector in Q3 still increased by 27% year-on-year, and the cumulative increase for the first nine months of the year was 121% year-on-year. On the one hand, the challenging real estate market amidst rising interest rates has significantly impacted the implementation schedule of projects and the capital costs of businesses. On the other hand, the huge demand for capital for projects will continue to be an important driving force for real estate businesses to increase bond issuance in the coming period.
 Bank bond issuance still increased by 7% compared to the previous quarter, but the cumulative figure for the first nine months was still 20% lower than the same period last year. The decline in bank bonds is also a significant reason for the slowdown in bond market growth.
 High capital demand will continue to drive the bond market in 2027.
 Entering the fourth quarter of 2026, S&I Ratings analysts believe that pressure from corporate bond maturing will increase significantly, with the total value of bonds due for payment estimated at approximately VND 93,000 billion, the highest level this year.
 In particular, the real estate sector continues to face the greatest pressure, with maturing loans valued at approximately VND 46,900 billion, equivalent to nearly half of the total maturing loans across the entire market. This maturing pressure is expected to continue into 2027 and will not end in 2026.
 According to estimates by S&I Ratings, the total value of corporate bonds maturing in 2027 could reach approximately VND 276 trillion, a 22% increase compared to 2026.
 Of that amount, the real estate sector alone accounted for VND 156 trillion, equivalent to 57% of the total market maturity value. New issuances in the coming period will not only meet the capital raising needs for new projects but also play a crucial role in restructuring existing debts.
 Besides the pressure of maturity, the economy 's demand for medium and long-term capital is entering a strong growth cycle to finance a series of large-scale real estate, urban development, transportation infrastructure, energy, and industrial projects. In this context, corporate bonds continue to be expected as an important capital raising channel to supplement medium and long-term resources for the economy.
 However, the high interest rate environment is expected to persist for at least the first half of 2027. For issuing companies, this means increased costs of capital, especially for companies with high leverage ratios or large capital raising needs.
 Nevertheless, the medium-term outlook for the corporate bond market remains positive due to the strong demand for capital from the corporate sector and increasing refinancing pressure.
 "In the context of still high interest rates, the corporate bond market needs more time to continue its restructuring process towards sustainability, attracting a wider range of investors, and assuming the role of a key medium- and long-term capital channel for the economy," the group of analysts commented.

articles.title: Banks are looking for room to lower interest rates through cost-cutting measures. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Banks are looking for room to lower interest rates through cost-cutting measures.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
According to statistics from the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV), as of October 19, 2026, capital mobilization by credit institutions increased by 11.22%, while credit increased by 11.44%. After several months of slower growth compared to credit, capital mobilization has gradually caught up with the growth rate of outstanding loans, narrowing the gap between the two indicators, improving the balance of capital sources and supporting the liquidity of the banking system.
 Mr. Nguyen Duc Lenh, Deputy Director of the State Bank of Vietnam's Regional Branch 2, said that this development has a positive impact on the monetary market and banking operations, contributing to ensuring the fulfillment of monetary policy objectives, especially the orientation of stabilizing interest rates to support businesses, households, and cooperatives, thereby promoting economic growth.
 In Ho Chi Minh City and Dong Nai, the capital mobilization activities of credit institutions also experienced high growth rates. In the first nine months of 2026, capital mobilization by credit institutions in the area increased by 11.72%, higher than the credit growth rate of 11.32% during the same period.
 Banks simultaneously cut interest rates.
 Following the directives of the Government and the Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam on reducing interest rates, as of October 20th, many more commercial banks have announced programs or plans to reduce lending interest rates, with common reductions ranging from 1.5–2 percentage points per year.
 Vietcombank announced a program to reduce interest rates from October 19th to December 31st, 2026, with a reduction of 1.5–2 percentage points per year in lending rates. Some short-term loans in priority sectors will receive a reduction of up to 3 percentage points compared to current rates. Simultaneously, the bank is reducing listed deposit interest rates by 0.5 percentage points per year for terms of 6 months or more to further facilitate lower capital costs. 
|  | 
| Banks are drastically reducing interest rates to attract customers to borrow capital for production and business activities at the end of the year. | 
 Along with other major banks, BVBank also adjusted down its listed deposit interest rates by 0.5 percentage points per year for terms from 6 to 24 months.
 At MB, the interest rate reduction program focuses on five priority areas: agriculture and rural areas; exports; small and medium-sized enterprises; supporting industries; and high-tech enterprises. The announced reduction is 1.5 percentage points per year, bringing the preferential lending interest rate down to 7.9% per year. Some other programs offer reductions of up to 2 percentage points, depending on the target group and loan conditions.
 Sacombank also allocated a credit package of VND 40,000 billion with a 2 percentage point annual reduction and preferential interest rates starting from 8.5% per year, focusing on businesses in key economic sectors, import-export, and foreign-invested enterprises. The bank stated that it has narrowed its profit margin from approximately 2.79% to 0.79% to implement the support program for import-export customers from mid-August to the end of 2026.
 In the small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) segment, Vietbank is implementing a VND 3,000 billion credit package from October 19, 2026 to June 30, 2027, or until the limit is reached, with interest rates at least 1.5 percentage points lower per year than the usual rate. For the agriculture, forestry, and fisheries sectors, the bank designs short-term loans suitable for the production and business cycle.
 In addition, BIDV, Agribank, VietinBank, SHB, TPBank, and LPBank have also announced interest rate reduction programs targeting production, business, and priority sectors. New disbursements are the main focus of many programs, while some banks are considering reducing interest rates for existing customers. The actual level of preferential rates depends on the term, purpose of capital use, and credit conditions of each bank.
 Most interest rate reduction programs are designed for specific customer groups, business sectors, and loan terms, rather than being applied uniformly to all outstanding loans. This approach reflects the banks' need to balance resources as credit demand increases at the end of the year, while also ensuring risk control and efficient capital utilization.
 Actively mobilizing capital creates additional conditions to support growth.
 Analyzing capital mobilization activities, Mr. Nguyen Duc Lenh, Deputy Director of the State Bank of Vietnam's Regional Branch 2, stated that the growth of mobilized capital is also linked to positive developments in domestic investment activities and attracting foreign investment, reflecting the capital circulation process and the economy's ability to absorb capital.
 Furthermore, macroeconomic stability, the convenience of banking services, and the efficiency of deposit channels continue to positively impact capital mobilization activities. These are also important conditions for credit institutions to exploit and utilize capital more effectively.
 According to Mr. Leinh, these positive developments, along with the year-end growth trend across all sectors of the economy, will facilitate credit institutions in meeting the capital needs for production, business, and economic growth in the final months of the year.
 However, economic experts believe that the ability to lower lending interest rates depends not only on the scale of mobilized capital but also on input costs, operational efficiency, and profit margins of each bank.
 According to Dr. Chau Dinh Linh, a lecturer at the Ho Chi Minh City University of Banking, lending interest rates are determined by several factors, including the cost of capital mobilization, operating costs, risk premium, and profit margin. Given the continued pressure on input capital costs, banks can still find room to reduce interest rates through cost reductions, improved management efficiency, technology application, and sharing a portion of profits with customers.
 Mr. Tran Van Linh, Chairman of the Board of Directors of Thuan Phuoc Seafood Joint Stock Company, assessed that the government's directive to reduce lending interest rates is a positive signal for production and business activities, especially during a period when businesses are having to balance many expenses to maintain and expand operations.
 According to Mr. Linh, rising raw material and production costs, coupled with limited purchasing power in export markets, are putting pressure on the business performance of enterprises.
 For the seafood industry, capital requirements often fluctuate according to the cycles of raw material procurement, processing, and order fulfillment. Therefore, interest rate reduction programs with appropriate terms and conditions tailored to the specifics of production will help businesses reduce financial costs and proactively manage capital during the peak production and export period at the end of the year.

articles.title: SHB unveils sustainable finance framework to expand green and social lending - vietnamnews.vn
articles.summary: SHB unveils sustainable finance framework to expand green and social lending  vietnamnews.vn
articles.full_text:
| SHB unveils its Sustainable Finance Framework. — Photos courtesy of SHB | 
HÀ NỘI — Saigon-Hanoi Commercial Joint Stock Bank (SHB) has unveiled its Sustainable Finance Framework (SFF), establishing criteria for identifying, assessing and selecting eligible projects for sustainable financing.
In early October, S&P Global Ratings issued an independent Second-Party Opinion (SPO) on the framework. According to the assessment, eligible green and social projects could help address major challenges facing Việt Nam, including rising carbon emissions, water stress and marine plastic pollution. Improving access to education, healthcare, credit and housing could also enhance living conditions and opportunities for disadvantaged groups.
An SPO assesses a financial framework at a specific point in time and is not a credit rating of the bank. It provides investors and financial institutions with an additional reference for evaluating fund allocation criteria, project selection processes and reporting mechanisms.
SHB’s framework standardises the management of funds allocated to sustainable activities and covers bonds, corporate loans, trade finance, consumer lending, and green, social and sustainability deposits.
It encompasses three categories: green finance, blue finance and social finance, linking capital allocation to environmental protection, natural resource conservation and improved quality of life.
Eligible green projects include renewable energy, energy efficiency, green buildings, clean transportation, pollution control, the circular economy and natural resource management. Blue finance focuses on marine ecosystem protection, sustainable water management, wastewater treatment, sustainable fisheries and responsible ocean-related economic activities.
Social finance covers access to finance, job creation, healthcare, education, affordable housing and basic infrastructure, aligning funding with specific economic and community needs.
| SHB seeks to channel capital into green projects and sustainable development. | 
The framework follows the International Capital Market Association’s Green Bond Principles, Social Bond Principles and Sustainability Bond Guidelines, alongside the Green Loan Principles and Social Loan Principles developed by the LMA, LSTA and APLMA. It also references the International Finance Corporation’s Guidelines for Blue Finance.
Under the framework, SHB has established procedures for project selection, appraisal and approval, applies an environmental and social management system to monitor risks, and specifies activities excluded from financing.
The bank has committed to publishing annual fund allocation and impact reports until all proceeds have been allocated. It will also engage an independent third party to review post-issuance allocation reports.
These measures aim to improve transparency and accountability, allowing stakeholders to track fund utilisation and assess results against published criteria. They also provide a basis for SHB to improve impact measurement, enhance environmental and social data quality, and develop products supporting customers’ investment, technological innovation and business transformation.
SHB recently announced a loan agreement coordinated by Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, with an initial facility of US$340 million that could be increased subject to the agreement’s terms.
The bank also successfully issued Singapore dollar-denominated bonds internationally for the first time. Listed on the Singapore Exchange, the bonds received a long-term “AA” issue credit rating from S&P Global Ratings before issuance. The rating applies to the bonds guaranteed by the Credit Guarantee and Investment Facility (CGIF), a trust fund of the Asian Development Bank, and reflects its unconditional, timely and irrevocable guarantee. It is not a credit rating of SHB itself.
The transaction helps diversify SHB’s medium- and long-term funding sources and expand relationships with international financial institutions and investors.
| SHB has received Global Finance’s “Best Sustainable Finance Bank in Việt Nam” title for several consecutive years. | 
Green credit targets and sustainable development
SHB aims to increase green credit to at least 25 per cent of its total outstanding loans by 2028.
Its renewable energy portfolio includes the 155MW Chợ Long wind power project, the 72MW Hoa Đông 2 wind power project and the 240MW Thiên Tân solar power complex. The three projects have a combined investment value of approximately VNĐ14.601 trillion, with SHB providing around VNĐ11.265 trillion in financing.
The bank has also raised two US dollar-denominated syndicated loans linked to environmental, social and governance (ESG) criteria, worth nearly $600 million in total, with participation from 26 international financial institutions.
In social finance, SHB prioritises small- and medium-sized enterprises, including women-owned businesses and companies participating in supply chains. Cooperation with international institutions also helps mobilise funding and technical assistance to improve credit access for target customer groups.
The framework and S&P Global Ratings’ independent opinion mark a step towards standardising how SHB identifies, manages and reports sustainable finance activities. They support the bank’s efforts to align lending with environmental and social objectives, strengthen disclosure and access a broader range of domestic and international funding sources.
The approach is in line with the spirit of Politburo Resolution No 59-NQ/TW on international integration in the new situation, reflecting SHB’s efforts to adopt international practices, expand partnerships and mobilise capital to support economic development. — VNS

articles.title: Tay Ninh, Vinh Long court stronger partnerships with China's Hong Kong - Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.summary: Tay Ninh, Vinh Long court stronger partnerships with China's Hong Kong  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Tay Ninh (VNA) – Authorities from Vietnam’s southern provinces of Tay Ninh and Vinh Long, in coordination with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Hong Kong Business Association Vietnam (HKBAV), held a dialogue in Ho Chi Minh City on October 19, seeking to draw investment, widen markets and deepen business ties.
The two provinces used the forum to pitch their advantages, development plans and priority investment areas. Hong Kong companies scouted opportunities in agriculture, food processing, industry, logistics, renewable energy and supply chains.
Pham Dut Diem, Director of the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Foreign Affairs, said Vietnam-Hong Kong (China) ties have flourished, with economy, trade, investment and tourism the standouts. Vietnam is now Hong Kong’s second largest trade partner in ASEAN and seventh largest globally, while Hong Kong is Vietnam’s seventh largest trade partner and fifth largest foreign investor.
He said Vietnam is pursuing rapid, sustainable growth while keeping the macroeconomy stable amid fast, complex changes in the global economy. It is targeting double-digit growth in 2026-2030, with science-technology, innovation and digital transformation as the bedrock.
Vietnam is seeking projects that bring advanced technology, modern management know-how, research and development and skilled labour, along with tighter links to domestic firms, Diem said. He urged Hong Kong companies to build stronger ties with Tay Ninh and Vinh Long in agriculture, processing, exports, logistics and financial services, and invest in industry, high technology and green, modern industrial parks. The localities must keep improving planning, infrastructure, land clearance, workforce, administrative reform and business climate to help investors roll out projects.
Xu Zhou, Acting Consul General of China in Ho Chi Minh City, said Hong Kong’s strengths lie in finance, trade, maritime transport, professional services and a broad international business network, making it a bridge between mainland China and global markets.
Tay Ninh and Vinh Long, meanwhile, have strong agricultural bases and industrial ambitions, along with a growing need to upgrade logistics and supply chain capacity. That leaves room for cooperation in agricultural processing, exports, manufacturing and infrastructure.
Xu said a growing number of Hong Kong firms have invested, launched startups and operated in southern Vietnam in warehousing, logistics, agriculture and manufacturing. The projects have created jobs, supported local growth and used Hong Kong’s connectivity networks to carry Vietnamese products to international markets.
The Consulate General stands ready to support economic, trade, cultural and people-to-people exchanges between Hong Kong and Vietnamese localities, Xu said, urging companies on both sides to play to their complementary strengths, pinpoint specific opportunities and turn discussions into projects.
Tay Ninh and Vinh Long, for their part, named wider international cooperation, quality investment attraction and better competitiveness as priorities for their new growth phase.
Dang Van Chinh, Standing Vice Chairman of the Vinh Long provincial People’s Committee, said the province aims to become a marine economy and renewable energy export hub in the Mekong Delta. It is prioritising green agriculture, deep processing, industrial park infrastructure, logistics, renewable energy and trade.
Vinh Long’s exports to Hong Kong reached 8.9 million USD in 2025, up 14% from a year earlier, and totaled 8.2 million USD in the first nine months of 2026, up 22.94%. Main products were footwear, apparel, seafood, coconut water and coconut milk.
According to Chinh, trade remains small relative to the local potential. Vinh Long wants direct links with Hong Kong importers, distributors and service providers to widen consumer markets and advance trade finance, payment services and e-commerce.
The province also seeks partners to develop raw-material zones and upgrade preservation, processing, packaging and traceability, as well as investment in logistics hubs, cold storage and distribution systems. In energy, it is looking for capital for nearshore and offshore wind power and green projects tied to technological innovation and digital transformation.
To back those goals, Vinh Long pledged an open, transparent and stable investment environment, public disclosure of planning information, project lists and land-access conditions, faster administrative reform and hands-on support for investors from site survey through project launch.
Truong Thanh Liem, Vice Chairman of the Tay Ninh provincial People’s Committee, said the local geographical location, border gate system and links to Long An International Port give it an edge in industry, logistics, border gate economy and trade with Cambodia and ASEAN.
Tay Ninh’s economy topped 14 billion USD in 2025, and its gross regional domestic product (GRDP) grew 10.3% in the first nine months of 2026. The province has attracted more than 2,100 foreign direct investment (FDI) projects from 50 countries and territories, with registered capital above 27 billion USD.
It targets annual GRDP growth of 10-10.5% through 2030, with the digital economy making up 30% of output. To realise the goal, it plans to reorganise its economic space, expand its network of industrial clusters and foster links among production, urban areas, border gates and ports.
Priority sectors include electronic components, semiconductors, precision engineering, agricultural processing, pharmaceuticals, medical equipment and biotechnology, along with urban development, trade, services, logistics, ecotourism, spiritual tourism and high-tech agriculture. The province also plans to diversify energy supply, develop renewables and step up cooperation on quality workforce training.
Tay Ninh pledges to support investors from initial scouting through project rollout and operation, supply information on planning and investment sites, guide them through procedures and work to clear obstacles in line with regulations, Liem said.
HKBAV Chairman Michael Chiu Kam Kwong said Tay Ninh and Vinh Long each have distinct strengths and opportunities, while Hong Kong offers international connectivity, financial capacity, logistics capabilities and professional services. Pairing them would open practical opportunities in trade, investment, food processing, infrastructure and supply chains.
Chiu said he hopes the dialogue will help companies find suitable partners, share information and build long-term ties. HKBAV will keep acting as a bridge, helping Hong Kong and Vietnamese enterprises expand their networks and tap opportunities in global and regional markets.
Tay Ninh and Vinh Long hope that the dialogue will deepen ties with Hong Kong companies and turn their advantages in location, raw materials, industry and energy into concrete projects. The goal is to widen markets, add value to products and support greener, more sustainable growth./.

Anwar also took aim at a former MP “who raised the matter but remained silent when he was serving as a minister”.
“This is why I tell my friends in Cabinet to use their powers properly to fix things and (not to wait) until they are retired or on the opposition bench to speak up on issues,” he added.
Separately, Anwar pledged to make public within three months the findings of a special multi-agency task force, led by attorney-general Dusuki Mokhtar, investigating allegations of a corporate mafia.
He said the task force involved MACC, the police, Bank Negara Malaysia, the Securities Commission, Inland Revenue Board and anti-money laundering enforcement units.
“It doesn’t matter whether the names mentioned are Azam, Farhash, or Victor Chin,” he said.
“But let us obtain full disclosure through the special committee headed by the attorney-general.”
He also said that the police’s anti-money laundering investigation team had frozen RM4.3 billion in funds and seized RM1 billion in assets linked to alleged corporate crimes between late 2022 and September 2026.
He said enforcement action during the same period also resulted in the forfeiture of RM48.3 million in assets and the issuance of compounds totalling RM1.1 billion.
He was responding to Aminuddin Harun (PH-Port Dickson), who asked for an update on allegations of “corporate mafia” activities involving violations of the law and the enforcement measures taken against those involved.

articles.title: Vietnam Airlines to launch direct Hanoi–Hangzhou flights in November - vietnamnews.vn
articles.summary: Vietnam Airlines to launch direct Hanoi–Hangzhou flights in November  vietnamnews.vn
articles.full_text:
| Flights will operate on Mondays, Thursdays, Fridays and Sundays using Airbus A321 aircraft, with a flight time of approximately three hours. — Photo courtesy of Vietnam Airlines | 
HÀ NỘI — Vietnam Airlines will launch a direct service between Hà Nội and Hangzhou, a major economic, technology and tourism hub in eastern China, on November 15, with four round-trip flights per week.
The new route will give travellers more convenient access to the Chinese city while creating additional opportunities for trade and tourism between Việt Nam and China. Flights will operate on Mondays, Thursdays, Fridays and Sundays using Airbus A321 aircraft, with a flight time of approximately three hours.
With the addition of Hangzhou, Vietnam Airlines will operate seven direct routes between Việt Nam and China, connecting the two countries through four cities: Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Hangzhou.
Nguyễn Quang Trung, deputy general director of Vietnam Airlines, said the new service marked another step in the carrier’s strategy to expand its international network.
“Despite ongoing market challenges, particularly fuel price fluctuations, bringing the route into operation earlier than planned, in the fourth quarter of 2026, demonstrates the airline’s proactive approach and determination to expand international connectivity,” he said.
The route was expected to facilitate trade and tourism while contributing to national economic growth, he added.
Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang Province, is known for West Lake, Longjing tea and the distinctive cultural heritage of the Jiangnan region. It is also a major centre for technology, e-commerce and innovation in China, home to the headquarters of several large businesses.
Located in the Yangtze River Delta, Hangzhou also provides a convenient base for exploring other destinations in eastern China, including Shanghai and cities across the Jiangnan region known for their cultural and historical attractions.
Since the beginning of 2026, Vietnam Airlines has continued to expand its international network, launching services to Amsterdam, Colombo, Phuket and Ahmedabad. The carrier has also increased frequencies on several routes to Seoul, Tokyo, Osaka, Taipei and Kaohsiung in Taiwan (China), Singapore, Manila, Moscow, Melbourne and Sydney.
The expansion reflects the airline’s efforts to strengthen international connectivity and broaden cooperation opportunities. Direct air links are expected to support trade, attract international visitors and enhance Việt Nam’s connections with key markets in the region and beyond. — VNS

| A representative from Phenikaa Group poses for a photo after receiving the title. — Photos courtesy of the group | 
HÀ NỘI — Phenikaa Group has received the Vietnam National Brand designation for its VICOSTONE engineered stone products for the fifth consecutive time, highlighting its investment in technology, innovation and sustainable manufacturing.
The recognition was announced at the 10th Vietnam National Brand ceremony, organised by the Ministry of Industry and Trade. Phenikaa first received the designation in 2018.
The 2026 selection process placed greater emphasis on innovation and creativity, including research and development, technology adoption, intellectual property protection, digital transformation and the green economy.
Phenikaa said it has invested in research and technology development throughout its 16-year history, seeking to strengthen its competitiveness by developing proprietary expertise and improving production efficiency.
The group operates seven engineered stone production lines with combined annual capacity of more than 3.5 million square metres, as well as two fabrication facilities with annual capacity of 500,000 square metres.
It also operates a cristobalite plant and a chemical plant producing unsaturated polyester resin. The company said both facilities use technology developed, designed and operated by its own experts and scientists.
Phenikaa has localised and mastered more than 95 per cent of its raw material inputs, making it one of the few engineered stone manufacturers globally to achieve that level of localisation, it said.
The group has also integrated multi-axis robotic automation systems into its production operations to improve efficiency and meet quality and design requirements in international markets.
Alongside investment in technology, Phenikaa said its Kaizen-5S continuous improvement programme, introduced in 2015, generated 1,699 initiatives in industrial production in 2025, creating value of more than 5.24 billion dong (US$199,000).
The company said the programme encouraged employees to identify operational issues and improve productivity, product quality and resource efficiency.
Product development
| One of Phenikaa's engineered stone product. | 
Phenikaa said its product development strategy aimed to combine technological advances with designs that meet customer demand for durable, visually distinctive materials and nature-inspired interiors.
The company said its investment in research, manufacturing technology and continuous improvement was intended to strengthen product value and operational efficiency amid intensifying international competition.
According to Phenikaa, it is also expanding its range of environmentally friendly products while increasing the use of recycled materials in production.
It added that the fifth consecutive national brand recognition will support further investment in innovation, new materials and smart manufacturing, with environmental, social and governance (ESG) principles guiding its development strategy.
The group also aims to achieve net-zero emissions, as it seeks to strengthen VICOSTONE's position in international markets and contribute to raising the profile of Vietnamese brands globally. — VNS

articles.title: Malaysia - Resources, Economy, Tourism - Britannica
articles.summary: Malaysia - Resources, Economy, Tourism  Britannica
articles.full_text:
Malaysia is rich in mineral resources, and mining (including petroleum extraction) accounts for a significant portion of GDP, although it employs only a tiny fraction of the workforce. The major metallic ores are tin, bauxite (aluminum), copper, and iron. A host of minor ores found within the country include manganese, antimony, mercury, and gold. Tin is found largely in alluvial deposits along the western slopes of the Main Range in Peninsular Malaysia, with smaller deposits on the east coast of the peninsula; its production formed one of the pillars of the country’s economic development in the mid-20th century. Malaysia’s bauxite production is centred near Johor at the south end of the peninsula, while the country’s copper comes from western Sabah.
News •
Since the 1970s, tin output has declined dramatically because of the depletion of readily accessible alluvial deposits, rising mining costs, and fluctuating demand in the world tin market. Nevertheless, the country has remained among the world’s top suppliers of tin. Production of other minerals (except petroleum) similarly decreased during the last decades of the 20th century, although the mining of iron ore began to rebound in the mid-1990s.
Malaysia’s most valuable mineral resources are its reserves of petroleum and natural gas. Crude oil, refined petroleum, and, more recently, liquefied natural gas together account for a major portion of the country’s commodity export earnings. Almost all the major oil and gas fields are offshore—off the east coast of the peninsula, the northeast coast of Sarawak, and the west coast of Sabah.
Malaysia is self-sufficient in energy production, and petroleum resources constitute the major energy source for power generation. The country’s proven reserves of coal and peat are not economical to mine and have remained largely unexploited. Wood and charcoal were once common domestic fuels, but in the urban areas they have been replaced by bottled gas. A small portion of Malaysia’s power is generated by hydroelectric plants, mostly on the peninsula. The abundant rainfall and steep gradients of the rivers in the interior highlands of both Peninsular and East Malaysia hold great potential for further hydroelectric development; in Sarawak, construction of a large hydroelectric dam on the Balui River began in the 1990s and continued into the 21st century. Malaysia also has begun to produce biofuel from palm oil.
Manufacturing
Manufacturing has undergone rapid expansion since the 1970s, with the aim of producing goods for export, while shifting away from import substitution (a policy of replacing imported products with those made domestically). By the early 21st century the sector had become the backbone of Malaysia’s economic growth, constituting the largest share (nearly one-third) of the country’s GDP and employing more of the workforce than all the primary activities (e.g., agriculture and mining) combined.
Growth has been especially notable in the assembly of electronic equipment, electrical machinery, and appliances, as well as in the production of chemicals and textiles. There also has been substantial development of a variety of heavy industries, including steelmaking and automobile production—the latter implemented through a Malaysian-Japanese joint venture. Peninsular Malaysia, especially the urban area of Kuala Lumpur and the rest of the developed zone along the western side of the peninsula, is responsible for the bulk of the country’s manufacturing output.
One strategy designed to promote manufactured exports has been the establishment of a number of free-trade zones, which have provided duty-free access to imported raw materials and semifinished parts in addition to numerous investment and export incentives. Industrial estates also have been established in less-developed parts of the country to stimulate manufacturing and to balance industrial growth, but manufacturing capacity has remained highly concentrated. The country’s heavy industries—more important politically than economically—generally have been saddled with excess capacity and high production costs. Increasingly, development strategy has shifted to the promotion of small and medium industries that manufacture their own parts and acquire technology from more economically developed countries, the aim being to move beyond the stage of assembly-only manufacturing. Such initiatives have enabled Malaysian industries such as automobile manufacturing to move from assembly-only production in the mid-1980s to full-fledged production—with minimal reliance on imported components—in the 21st century.
Finance
Malaysia has an active and growing financial sector, which has been encouraged by government policies that promote foreign investment, market competition, and the privatization of publicly held enterprises. Banking and insurance are regulated by the state-run Bank Negara Malaysia, which issues the national currency, the ringgit. The state permits a variety of banking activities, including semipublic banks that operate on Islamic financial principles. Since 1990 the island of Labuan, off the southwest coast of Sabah, has served as an international financial centre; a regulatory authority there issues offshore banking licenses. Kuala Lumpur has a commodity exchange and a stock exchange.
Trade
Malaysia’s export structure shifted dramatically during the last decades of the 20th century, from one dominated by rubber and tin to one in which manufactured goods accounted for well over half of all export earnings by the early 21st century. Electrical and electronic products constitute the largest proportion of exported manufactures. Commodities exports, however, especially palm oil and rubber, remain important. Imports are dominated by electronics parts, machinery, and other manufactured goods. Malaysia’s chief trading partners are Japan, Singapore (because of its status as an entrepôt port in the region), the United States, and China. Other prominent partners include Thailand, Taiwan, and South Korea. Malaysia belongs to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the World Trade Organization (WTO).
